### Summary

I know this has been discussed in great length already in various places, like https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/4048 

And I totally support your idea of having cmd+c to open the clean-cache dialog instead of copying. 

I'm just asking for small knob for me to set a different keyboard shortcut, because I don't want to always have to engage the viewer-mode just for my development purposes. 

I'm even happy with an undocumented little knob to inject something into the typescript components.

### Summary

There is no single way currently to verify Google Search Console in a deployed streamlit app on streamlit community cloud.

### Why?

Many developers need this for production apps with streamlit.

### How?

We would like a way to insert the meta tags into the ROOT <head> tag (not inside the isolated iframe) for GSC to detect. It would we also useful to add a description meta tag.

### Additional Context

Thank You!

body_text:
### Checklist

- [X] I have searched the existing issues for similar feature requests.
- [X] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

When using `refresh_mode="background"` on `st.cache_data` / `st.cache_resource`, the stale grace window is fixed at 1×TTL (hard expiry at 2×TTL). This means an app idle overnight (longer than 2×TTL) has its cache evicted and the first morning user blocks on a cold miss.

A `max_stale` parameter would let users configure the stale grace window independently from TTL:

```python
@st.cache_data(ttl="2m", max_stale="12h", refresh_mode="background")
def load_data():
    return expensive_query()
```

This separates two concerns: **how often to refresh** (`ttl="2m"`) from **how long stale data is acceptable** (`max_stale="12h"`). Users who want frequent freshness checks but never want to block get exactly that.

### Why?

From [#11050](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/11050) (comment by @itsToggle):

> Is there any way that we can influence the "2 × ttl" background cache timeout? In my use case I want a short ttl so the values are updated often, but I never want my users to have to wait for a response. I would like to set the ttl to something like 2 minutes, but the oldest background cache that's allowed to be served can be much older than four minutes.

This is also the more practical solution for the "first user of the day" problem compared to cron scheduling, since it does not require an always-on server and works on scale-to-zero deployments.

### How?

The [background refresh spec](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/develop/specs/2026-04-08-cache-background-refresh/product-spec.md) already calls this out as future work:

> **`max_stale` parameter**: Explicitly configure the stale grace window (default: equal to `ttl`), e.g. `ttl="1h", max_stale="12h"` to serve stale data across an overnight idle gap without blocking the first morning user

### Additional Context

- Related (closed): [#5871](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/5871), [#11050](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/11050)

- [X] I have searched the existing issues for similar feature requests.
- [X] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

When using `refresh_mode="background"` on `st.cache_data` / `st.cache_resource`, the stale grace window is fixed at 1×TTL (hard expiry at 2×TTL). This means an app idle overnight (longer than 2×TTL) has its cache evicted and the first morning user blocks on a cold miss.

A `max_stale` parameter would let users configure the stale grace window independently from TTL:

```python
@st.cache_data(ttl="2m", max_stale="12h", refresh_mode="background")
def load_data():
    return expensive_query()
```

This separates two concerns: **how often to refresh** (`ttl="2m"`) from **how long stale data is acceptable** (`max_stale="12h"`). Users who want frequent freshness checks but never want to block get exactly that.

### Why?

From [#11050](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/11050) (comment by @itsToggle):

> Is there any way that we can influence the "2 × ttl" background cache timeout? In my use case I want a short ttl so the values are updated often, but I never want my users to have to wait for a response. I would like to set the ttl to something like 2 minutes, but the oldest background cache that's allowed to be served can be much older than four minutes.

This is also the more practical solution for the "first user of the day" problem compared to cron scheduling, since it does not require an always-on server and works on scale-to-zero deployments.

### How?

The [background refresh spec](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/develop/specs/2026-04-08-cache-background-refresh/product-spec.md) already calls this out as future work:

> **`max_stale` parameter**: Explicitly configure the stale grace window (default: equal to `ttl`), e.g. `ttl="1h", max_stale="12h"` to serve stale data across an overnight idle gap without blocking the first morning user

### Additional Context

- Related (closed): [#5871](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/5871), [#11050](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/11050)

In a simple dataframe with a long and a short text column, the long column is getting cropped while there is still enough whitespace behind the strings in the short column to manually adjust column width, such that everything fits.         "Short text": [
            "Lorem ipsum",
            "Dolor sit amet",
            "Consectetur adipiscing elit",
        ],

)

body_text: ### Checklist - [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar issues. - [x] I added a very descriptive title to this issue. - [x] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue. ### Summary A keyed `st.dataframe` or `st.data_editor` excludes its data from the element identity: `key_as_main_identity={"selection_mode", "is_selection_activated"}` at [arrow.py lines 1280-1284](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/2bd9d77e68e1ef6beaee2bcf98da2c0707bacc63/lib/streamlit/elements/arrow.py#L1280-L1284). The element id therefore survives a data refresh, and the browser resends grid state that was computed against the previous frame. `event.selection.rows` and `edited_rows` are positional, so after a rerun that reorders or inserts rows those positions address different records, and the app receives a selection or an edit for a row the user never touched. There is no error and no warning. The comment directly above that call site acknowledges that selections "can become orphaned when the data changes" and that resetting them "might be a nice enhancement"; the effect on an app that acts on the selection is a wrong-row write, not a cosmetic orphan. ### Reproducible Code Example ```Python import pandas as pd import streamlit as st st.session_state.setdefault("gen", 0) st.session_state.setdefault("closed", []) # Simulates a queue whose contents change between reruns (a new ticket arrived). rows = ["TICK-101", "TICK-102", "TICK-103", "TICK-104"] if st.session_state["gen"]: rows = ["TICK-100", *rows] df = pd.DataFrame({"ticket": rows}) event = st.dataframe(df, key="queue", on_select="rerun", selection_mode="single-row") if st.button("Simulate new ticket arriving", key="refresh"): st.session_state["gen"] += 1 st.rerun() if st.button("Close selected", key="close") and event.selection.rows: position = event.selection.rows[0] st.session_state["closed"].append(df.iloc[position]["ticket"]) st.write("Selected positions:", event.selection.rows) st.write("Closed:", st.session_state["closed"]) ``` ### Steps To Reproduce 1. `streamlit run` (or `uv run streamlit run`) the snippet. 2. Click the row showing `TICK-102` (position 1). The app shows `Selected positions: [1]`. 3. Click "Simulate new ticket arriving". `TICK-102` gets bumped down to position 2, but the highlighted row and `event.selection.rows` are still `[1]`, which is now `TICK-101`. 4. Click "Close selected". You get `Closed: ['TICK-101']` even though you had initially selected `TICK-102`. The same holds for `st.data_editor` with the default `num_rows="fixed"`: a pending `edited_rows` entry is re-applied at the same position after the frame changes. The identity part can be shown without a browser, using `AppTest`: ```python from streamlit.testing.v1 import AppTest def script(): import pandas as pd import streamlit as st st.session_state.setdefault("gen", 0) if st.button("refresh", key="refresh"): st.session_state["gen"] += 1 rows = ["TICK-101", "TICK-102", "TICK-103", "TICK-104"] if st.session_state["gen"]: rows = ["TICK-100", *rows] df = pd.DataFrame({"ticket": rows}) st.dataframe(df, key="queue", on_select="rerun", selection_mode="single-row") st.dataframe(df, on_select="rerun", selection_mode="single-row") at = AppTest.from_function(script).run() keyed, unkeyed = at.dataframe[0].proto.id, at.dataframe[1].proto.id at.button(key="refresh").click().run() print(keyed == at.dataframe[0].proto.id) # True -> keyed id survives the data change print(unkeyed == at.dataframe[1].proto.id) # False -> unkeyed id does not ``` ### Expected Behavior When the data behind a keyed grid changes, stale selection and edit state should be reset (or the state should be keyed by row identity rather than position), so an app never receives positions computed against a frame it is no longer showing. At minimum the docs for `key=` on `st.dataframe` / `st.data_editor` should say that selection and edit state is positional and survives data changes. ### Current Behavior Positional selection and edit state is preserved across data changes for keyed grids. Dropping `key=` makes the id data-dependent and the stale state orphans to empty, which is safe but discards every pending selection or edit on any data change, and contradicts the general advice to always give widgets a key. ### Is this a regression? - [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version. Not a recent regression, at least. The row retarget in steps 1-4 was observed in Chromium on 1.60.0. The `AppTest` demonstration above prints `True` / `False` on both 1.63.0 and 1.64.0 (the latest release at the time of writing), and the identity code is unchanged at the current tip of `develop`. On 1.60.0 and later the `st.data_editor` case is wider than on 1.59.x: a keyed editor with `num_rows="fixed"` re-applies a pending edit at the same position after a reorder, where 1.59.x discarded it. ### Debug info - Streamlit version: 1.63.0 and 1.64.0, both reproduced - Python version: 3.14.6 - Operating System: Linux Mint 22.3 Zena 64-bit - Browser: Version 152.0.7977.82 (Official Build) for Linux Mint (x86_64) ### Additional Information Related: `_apply_dataframe_edits` ([data_editor.py#L560-L564](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/2bd9d77e68e1ef6beaee2bcf98da2c0707bacc63/lib/streamlit/elements/widgets/data_editor.py#L560-L564)) receives no `disabled` argument, so `disabled=["_index"]` is enforced only in the browser; a client-sent index edit is applied server-side. Apps that act on grid state currently have to pin the frame they rendered in `st.session_state`, resolve positions against that frame, and reject anything they did not serve.

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar issues.
- [x] I added a very descriptive title to this issue.
- [x] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue.

### Summary

`ForwardMsgQueue.clear(retain_lifecycle_msgs=True)` keeps only `new_session`, `script_finished`, `session_status_changed`, `parent_message`, `page_info_changed` and toast deltas ([forward_msg_queue.py lines 135-146](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/2bd9d77e68e1ef6beaee2bcf98da2c0707bacc63/lib/streamlit/runtime/forward_msg_queue.py#L135-L146)). `heartbeat_ack` is not in that set, so an ack that is already sitting in the queue is destroyed instead of delivered. `AppSession._clear_queue` calls this on every `SCRIPT_STARTED`, and the runtime flushes queues on a short timer, so an ack enqueued in the window between a heartbeat arriving and the next script run starting never reaches the browser. A host that sends one `SEND_APP_HEARTBEAT` and waits for the ack can wait forever.

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
from streamlit.proto.ForwardMsg_pb2 import ForwardMsg
from streamlit.runtime.forward_msg_queue import ForwardMsgQueue

queue = ForwardMsgQueue()

ack = ForwardMsg()
ack.heartbeat_ack = True
finished = ForwardMsg()
finished.script_finished = ForwardMsg.FINISHED_SUCCESSFULLY

queue.enqueue(ack)
queue.enqueue(finished)
[m.WhichOneof("type") for m in queue._queue]  # ['heartbeat_ack', 'script_finished']

queue.clear(retain_lifecycle_msgs=True)
[m.WhichOneof("type") for m in queue._queue]  # ['script_finished']  <- ack is gone
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. `streamlit run` (or `uv run streamlit run`) the snippet.
2. Observe that the second print no longer contains `heartbeat_ack`.

End to end: open an app in an iframe host that sends `SEND_APP_HEARTBEAT` exactly once while a rerun is being triggered (for example, immediately after a widget interaction). The ack for that heartbeat is never received.

### Expected Behavior

A heartbeat ack is a one-shot reply to a client request, like a toast is a one-shot notification. It should survive the interrupted-run queue clear, or be sent directly rather than queued, so that one heartbeat always produces one ack.

### Current Behavior

The ack is silently removed from the queue when a script run starts before the queue is flushed. Nothing is logged. The client sees no reply.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.63.0 and 1.64.0, both reproduced
- Python version: 3.14.6
- Operating System: Linux Mint 22.3 Zena 64-bit
- Browser: Version 152.0.7977.82 (Official Build) for Linux Mint (x86_64) but **not browser-specific; reproduced as a pure function of `ForwardMsgQueue`**

### Additional Information

The toast case (#7740) was fixed by adding `_is_toast_delta(msg)` to the retain predicate ([forward_msg_queue.py line 146](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/2bd9d77e68e1ef6beaee2bcf98da2c0707bacc63/lib/streamlit/runtime/forward_msg_queue.py#L146)); the same shape would fix this (`msg.WhichOneof("type") == "heartbeat_ack"`). We hit this from a test harness that uses a heartbeat round trip to prove a WebSocket reconnect completed; sending heartbeats on an interval rather than once is the workaround.

`ForwardMsgQueue.clear(retain_lifecycle_msgs=True)` keeps only `new_session`, `script_finished`, `session_status_changed`, `parent_message`, `page_info_changed` and toast deltas ([forward_msg_queue.py lines 135-146](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/2bd9d77e68e1ef6beaee2bcf98da2c0707bacc63/lib/streamlit/runtime/forward_msg_queue.py#L135-L146)). `heartbeat_ack` is not in that set, so an ack that is already sitting in the queue is destroyed instead of delivered. `AppSession._clear_queue` calls this on every `SCRIPT_STARTED`, and the runtime flushes queues on a short timer, so an ack enqueued in the window between a heartbeat arriving and the next script run starting never reaches the browser. A host that sends one `SEND_APP_HEARTBEAT` and waits for the ack can wait forever.

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
from streamlit.proto.ForwardMsg_pb2 import ForwardMsg
from streamlit.runtime.forward_msg_queue import ForwardMsgQueue

queue = ForwardMsgQueue()

ack = ForwardMsg()
ack.heartbeat_ack = True
finished = ForwardMsg()
finished.script_finished = ForwardMsg.FINISHED_SUCCESSFULLY

queue.enqueue(ack)
queue.enqueue(finished)
[m.WhichOneof("type") for m in queue._queue]  # ['heartbeat_ack', 'script_finished']

queue.clear(retain_lifecycle_msgs=True)
[m.WhichOneof("type") for m in queue._queue]  # ['script_finished']  <- ack is gone
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. `streamlit run` (or `uv run streamlit run`) the snippet.
2. Observe that the second print no longer contains `heartbeat_ack`.

End to end: open an app in an iframe host that sends `SEND_APP_HEARTBEAT` exactly once while a rerun is being triggered (for example, immediately after a widget interaction). The ack for that heartbeat is never received.

### Expected Behavior

A heartbeat ack is a one-shot reply to a client request, like a toast is a one-shot notification. It should survive the interrupted-run queue clear, or be sent directly rather than queued, so that one heartbeat always produces one ack.

### Current Behavior

The ack is silently removed from the queue when a script run starts before the queue is flushed. Nothing is logged. The client sees no reply.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.63.0 and 1.64.0, both reproduced
- Python version: 3.14.6
- Operating System: Linux Mint 22.3 Zena 64-bit
- Browser: Version 152.0.7977.82 (Official Build) for Linux Mint (x86_64) but **not browser-specific; reproduced as a pure function of `ForwardMsgQueue`**

### Additional Information

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar issues.

- [x] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue.

### Summary

On fresh page load (before any user interaction), st.pills (multi-select mode) renders ALL options with the "selected" purple-outline style in Safari, even though no option is selected — the underlying server-side state (default=None) is correctly empty. The visual bug appears specifically in real Safari and does not reproduce in Chromium or Playwright's WebKit engine.

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
import streamlit as st

selected = st.pills(
    "Filter",
    options=["Option A", "Option B", "Option C"],
    selection_mode="multi",
    default=None,
)
st.write(selected)
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Open the app fresh in Safari (macOS or iOS) — a new tab/window, not a warm reload.
2. Before clicking anything, observe the st.pills widget with selection_mode="multi" and default=None.
3. All options render with the "selected" purple-outline styling, even though nothing has been selected yet.
4. The underlying state is correct (st.write(selected) shows an empty list) — this is a visual-only bug.
5. Does NOT reproduce in Chromium or in Playwright's WebKit engine — only in real Safari.

### Expected Behavior

On fresh load with default=None, all pill options should render in the plain/unselected style, matching the actual empty selection state.

### Current Behavior

All pill options render in the "selected" style (purple outline/fill) on fresh page load in Safari, despite no option being selected and the server-side value correctly being an empty list.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.64.0
- Python version: (from your requirements.txt / Railway build — Claude Code can confirm the exact version)
- Browser: Safari (macOS) — reproduces on real Safari; does not reproduce in Chromium or Playwright's WebKit
- OS: macOS

### Additional Information

Extracted the relevant CSS from the live page's compiled stylesheet:
[data-selected]:not([data-disabled]) { background-color: rgba(79,70,229,0.1); border-color: rgb(79,70,229); color: rgb(79,70,229); }

This appears to be an attribute-presence selector issue: in Chromium/WebKit-via-Playwright, react-aria (the underlying ToggleButtonGroup implementation) correctly omits the data-selected attribute entirely on unselected buttons, so the selector doesn't match. It's possible real Safari's DOM/CSS engine handles react-aria's attribute timing differently on initial paint, causing data-selected to be briefly (or persistently) present on all buttons before Safari's own attribute-removal logic runs — worth investigating from the react-aria/Safari interaction side.

The visual bug appears specifically in real Safari and does not reproduce in Chromium or Playwright's WebKit engine.

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
import streamlit as st

selected = st.pills(
    "Filter",
    options=["Option A", "Option B", "Option C"],
    selection_mode="multi",
    default=None,
)
st.write(selected)
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Open the app fresh in Safari (macOS or iOS) — a new tab/window, not a warm reload.
2. Before clicking anything, observe the st.pills widget with selection_mode="multi" and default=None.
3. All options render with the "selected" purple-outline styling, even though nothing has been selected yet.
4. The underlying state is correct (st.write(selected) shows an empty list) — this is a visual-only bug.
5. Does NOT reproduce in Chromium or in Playwright's WebKit engine — only in real Safari.

### Expected Behavior

On fresh load with default=None, all pill options should render in the plain/unselected style, matching the actual empty selection state.

### Current Behavior

All pill options render in the "selected" style (purple outline/fill) on fresh page load in Safari, despite no option being selected and the server-side value correctly being an empty list.

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Add an opt-in `copy="cow"` mode to `st.cache_data` that uses copy-on-write semantics for cached return values. This avoids unnecessary full-object deserialization on cache hits while preserving isolation between callers, significantly reducing cache-hit latency and memory allocation for large cached objects.

### Why?

`st.cache_data` currently creates an independent copy of the cached value for each call. This provides isolation between callers, but for large objects such as Pandas DataFrames and NumPy arrays, repeatedly deserializing and copying cached values can introduce significant CPU time and memory allocation overhead.

This becomes particularly relevant for applications where large datasets are read repeatedly across multiple sessions, while mutations to returned values are relatively uncommon.

An opt-in copy-on-write mode can preserve the isolation guarantees of `st.cache_data` while avoiding unnecessary full-object duplication on cache hits. The existing behavior would remain unchanged for applications that do not opt into the new mode.

In benchmarks using Python 3.13.15, Pandas 3.0.6, and Streamlit 1.64.0, the prototype reduced observed cache-hit latency by approximately 2.7–3.2× for DataFrames ranging from 5,000 to 1,000,000 rows. In a separate allocation benchmark with 10 consecutive reads, observed allocation decreased from approximately 4.67 MB to 0.02–0.03 MB.

### How?

Introduce an optional `copy` parameter on `st.cache_data`:

```python
@st.cache_data(copy="cow")
def load_data():
    return pd.read_parquet("large_dataset.parquet")

### Additional Context

### Prototype

A working prototype is available in my fork:

https://github.com/Isllanrx/streamlit/tree/feature/cache-data-cow

The implementation is currently limited to the following areas:

- `st.cache_data` API support for `copy="cow"`
- Copy-on-write handling for supported cached return values
- Caller/session mutation isolation
- Integration with existing cache lifecycle and eviction behavior
- Unit tests for mutation isolation
- Static typing coverage for the public API

### Performance Benchmark

The prototype was benchmarked using Python 3.13.15, Pandas 3.0.6, and Streamlit 1.64.0.

| Dataset | Default copy | `copy="cow"` | Speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5,000 × 12 | 0.155 ms | 0.055 ms | 2.8× |
| 50,000 × 12 | 0.158 ms | 0.049 ms | 3.2× |
| 200,000 × 12 | 0.144 ms | 0.048 ms | 3.0× |
| 1,000,000 × 12 | 0.131 ms | 0.049 ms | 2.7× |

In a separate allocation benchmark using 10 consecutive cache reads, observed allocation decreased from approximately 4.67 MB with the existing behavior to approximately 0.02–0.03 MB with `copy="cow"`.

### Stress Testing

The implementation was also tested under concurrent mutation and cache lifecycle pressure:

| Scenario | Result |
| --- | --- |
| 50 concurrent threads mutating the same 100,000-row DataFrame | Passed |
| Nested dictionaries containing DataFrames, Series, and lists | Passed |
| 200 concurrent cache entries with `max_entries=5` | Passed |
| Concurrent readers while repeatedly calling `.clear()` | Passed |
| 1,000,000-row (~100 MB) DataFrame with mutation isolation | Passed |

The concurrent mutation test completed in approximately 0.046 seconds. The cached DataFrame remained unchanged and no cross-caller mutations were observed.

The 1,000,000-row test also preserved mutation isolation, with subsequent reads completing in approximately 0.08 ms.

These tests were specifically designed to validate both the performance characteristics and the isolation guarantees of the proposed copy-on-write behavior.

### Summary

`LinkColumn(display_text=":material/open_in_new:")` now renders correctly in narrow cells (see #14782 / #17090).

Every other `:material/...:` icon still uses the ligature-name path. Glide pre-truncates canvas text with `max = cellWidth / 4` before `fillText`, so an icon whose name is N characters still fails below about `4N` pixels. Example from #14782: `:material/signal_cellular_connected_no_internet_0_bar:` (43 characters) needs ~172px.

This is pre-existing, not a regression from #17090. 

A durable general fix likely belongs in Glide (`truncateString` vs canvas clipping). 

We may special-case additional high-traffic icons the same way as `open_in_new` if they show up in real apps.

### If this is affecting you

Please comment with:

1. The exact icon, e.g. `:material/open_in_browser:`
2. The `LinkColumn` `width` you are using
3. A short note on the use case if it is not “open this URL”


### Related

- Original report: #14782
- Scoped fix for `open_in_new`: #17090

### Summary

Currently, the cache decorators are just simple decorators of a hashable saving with the possibility of clearing the cache.

However, a key component in caching is when the cache was saved.

Currently the only method to now this is by caching the result with a timestamp, which is unpractical.

So I'm thinking about a ´´´cached_function.time()´´´ method for knowing when it was last cached.

### Why?

Because knowing the time of the cache would be very comprehensive for:
- Not clearing cache everytime an update is needed, checking first if the time of the cache is soon enough
- Simply adding a display of Last Updated at

### How?

When saving the cache save the timestamp as well and implement a .time method to the cached function for retrieving the time as a time.time() timestamp.

## Summary

Let a cached data source declare a cheap "has the source changed?" probe, so
Streamlit re-runs the expensive query (and updates dependent fragments) **only
when the underlying data actually changed** — instead of on a blind timer. This
is the event-driven counterpart to timer-based refresh.

## Why?

Timer-based refresh (`@st.fragment(run_every=…)`, or a server-side scheduled
refresh) fires on a fixed clock regardless of whether anything changed. For an
expensive query that forces a bad tradeoff:

- **Poll fast** → the heavy query re-runs every interval even when the data is
  identical, wasting warehouse/API cost.
- **Poll slow** → users stare at stale data between ticks.

Sources usually expose something *cheap* that reveals whether they changed — a
version token, an ETag, a `MAX(updated_at)`, a Snowflake stream or
change-tracking timestamp. There's no built-in way to poll that cheap signal
often and re-run the expensive work only when it moves.

## How?

Attach a cheap freshness function to a cached data source. Streamlit checks the
freshness token; when it changes, it invalidates the cache and re-runs the
fragments that read it. When it's unchanged, the cached value is served and no
expensive work runs.

Sketch (names illustrative):

```python
def orders_version():
    # Cheap probe — cache invalidates when this value changes.
    return conn.query("SELECT MAX(updated_at) FROM orders")

@st.cache_data(freshness=orders_version)
def load_orders():
    return conn.query("SELECT * FROM orders")   # expensive; runs only on change

@st.fragment(run_every="5s")
def orders_panel():
    df = load_orders()      # cheap probe each poll; heavy query only when changed
    st.line_chart(df, x="ts", y="orders")

orders_panel()
```

body_text:
## Summary

Provide a way to refresh a data source on a **server-side schedule** — computed
once for the whole app and pushed to every session currently viewing it —
instead of each session running its own `run_every` timer and recomputing the
same query independently. This is the shared "the dashboard refreshes every
minute and everyone sees the latest" pattern that live/ops dashboards need.

## Why?

`@st.fragment(run_every=…)` already gives time-driven updates, but the timer and
the computation are **per session**: with _N_ viewers on the same dashboard you
get _N_ timers and _N_ executions of the same query every interval. A refresh
that is cheap for one user becomes _N×_ load on the warehouse/API for a shared
internal tool.

`@st.cache_data` dedupes the *computation* across sessions, but nothing *drives*
a periodic refresh or *wakes* the sessions when a new value lands — today
`run_every` is the driver, and it's per session. The missing piece is a refresh
that runs once for the whole app and updates every session viewing it.

## How?

Mark a cached data source to refresh on a fixed interval, centrally for the
whole app. Any fragment that reads it shows the current value and re-renders when
a new one lands.

Sketch (names illustrative):

```python
# The value refreshes centrally every 60s; sessions read the current value and
# rerun when a new one lands — no per-session timer, one shared computation.
@st.cache_data(refresh_every="60s")
def latest_metrics():
    return run_warehouse_query()

@st.fragment
def kpis():
    df = latest_metrics()          # returns the current cached value immediately
    st.metric("Orders", len(df))
    st.line_chart(df, x="ts", y="orders")

kpis()
```

## Additional Context

- Split out from [#12980](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/12980)
  ("real-time chart updates without rerunning the entire script"), which is being
  closed now that fragments (`run_every`), `st.rerun(scope=…)`, and element
  diffing cover the original per-session/live-update and flicker concerns.
- Related in-flight work: the non-blocking background execution spec
  ([#17067](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/17067)) covers shared,
  off-thread cached computation; scheduled/recurring refresh is called out there
  as not-yet-built.
- Companion gap: a **freshness signal**
  ([#17141](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/17141)) — a cheap "did
  the source change?" probe (e.g. Snowflake change-tracking / `LAST_ALTERED` /
  `MAX(updated_at)`) to drive **event-driven** invalidation instead of a blind
  timer. That's the push counterpart to this timer-based one.

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Feature Proposal: From Rerun-Driven to Event-Driven Streamlit
The Core Idea

Streamlit's greatest strength is also one of its defining architectural characteristics: Python execution is the primary mechanism through which application state and UI are updated.

This works exceptionally well for data applications where an interaction naturally maps to a Python computation.

However, highly interactive applications expose a different requirement:

A browser event is not necessarily a Python execution event.

A mouse move, drag, hover, resize, crosshair movement, animation frame, realtime tick, or temporary UI state change may occur dozens or hundreds of times per second.

Most of these events should not require Python to rerun.

The proposal is therefore not simply to add more widgets or more rerun options.

The deeper proposal is to introduce a lightweight event/state runtime between the browser and Python execution model.

Instead of treating every interaction as:

UI event → Python → rerun → UI

Streamlit could support:

                         UI EVENT
                             │
                 ┌───────────┴───────────┐
                 │                       │
                 ▼                       ▼
          Client-side state        Event routing
                 │                       │
                 │              ┌────────┼────────┐
                 │              │        │        │
                 ▼              ▼        ▼        ▼
             UI update       Client   Fragment   App
                              only      rerun    rerun

Python would remain the primary application and business-logic layer, but it would no longer have to participate in every interaction.

This is the architectural distinction behind the rest of this proposal.

The objective is not to turn Streamlit into React.

The objective is to make Streamlit capable of supporting both:

Traditional Streamlit
interaction → Python rerun

and:

Highly interactive Streamlit
interaction → client/state/event layer → Python only when needed

The existing programming model would remain intact. The new model would simply provide a second level of control for applications that need it.

Streamlit has made significant progress toward more granular execution control, fragments, background execution, and real-time UI updates.

The next step could be to provide a more general event-driven interaction model that allows Streamlit applications to handle high-frequency client-side events and state changes without requiring a Python script rerun for every interaction.

This would make Streamlit much more suitable not only for dashboards and data applications, but also for highly interactive applications such as trading terminals, monitoring systems, visual editors, control panels, and real-time operational interfaces.

The goal is not to replace Streamlit's existing rerun model, but to add a second, more granular interaction layer alongside it.

---

# The Core Problem

Today, Streamlit provides an excellent Python-first programming model:

User interaction
      ↓
Widget event
      ↓
Python execution
      ↓
UI update

This model is extremely productive for traditional data applications.
However, highly interactive applications often have a different event profile:

Mouse movement
Drag
Resize
Hover
Crosshair movement
Keyboard shortcut
Realtime market tick
Chart event
Component state change
      ↓
potentially dozens or hundreds of events per second

Not every one of these events should require a Python rerun.

For example, dragging a trading order line from one price to another may generate many intermediate browser events, while the application may only need to execute Python logic when the user releases the mouse button.

Similarly, a chart crosshair can move continuously without requiring Python execution at every pixel.

A more explicit separation between **client-side interaction**, **application state**, and **Python execution** would make Streamlit considerably more powerful.

# Proposed Model
Introduce an event/state layer that allows developers to explicitly define what happens when a client-side event occurs.

Conceptually:

                    ┌─────────────────────┐
                    │      Browser        │
                    │                     │
                    │ UI / Chart / Input  │
                    └──────────┬──────────┘
                               │
                    Client-side events
                               │
              ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
              │                │                │
              ▼                ▼                ▼
          Client state     Event stream     Python event
              │                │                │
              ▼                ▼                ▼
       No rerun needed    Optional rerun    Fragment/App

The important idea is that **an event should not automatically imply a Python rerun**.

# 1. True Client-Side State

Allow components to maintain state that can change frequently on the client without immediately triggering Python execution.

For example:

chart_state = st.chart(
    symbol="BTCUSDT",
    client_state=True
)

Client-side state could include:

* cursor position
* selected item
* drag position
* zoom level
* viewport
* temporary form state
* hover state
* drawing state
* component-local UI state

Python could explicitly request the current state when needed.

This would preserve Streamlit's Python-first model while allowing components to behave more like native browser applications.

# 2. Event Channels

Introduce a generic event mechanism for high-frequency or transient browser events.
For example:

[python]
chart.on("mousemove", handler)
chart.on("drag", handler)
chart.on("crosshair", handler)
chart.on("resize", handler)
chart.on("selection", handler)

Events should be distinguishable from persistent state.
A useful distinction could be:

State
→ "What is the current value?"

Event
→ "What just happened?"
```
This distinction is particularly important for transient events such as mouse movement, clicks, keyboard shortcuts, and drag operations.

# 3. Fire-and-Forget Events

Allow events to be processed entirely on the client without invoking Python.
For example:

[python]
chart.on(
    "mousemove",
    client=True
)
or conceptually:

[python]
chart.on("drag", rerun=False)

This would allow extremely frequent UI interactions without overwhelming the Streamlit execution engine.
Python could still receive the final result:

drag start
   ↓
client-side movement
   ↓
client-side movement
   ↓
client-side movement
   ↓
drag end
   ↓
Python event

This is especially useful for:

* chart interactions
* sliders
* drawing tools
* drag-and-drop
* resizing
* visual editors
* canvas applications

# 4. Explicit Rerun Policy

Allow developers to explicitly define the execution scope of an event.
For example, conceptually:

[python]
widget(
    on_change="client"
)

or:

[python]
widget(
    on_event="fragment"
)

or:

[python]
widget(
    on_event="app"
)

or:

[python]
widget(
    on_event="none"
)

The exact API is open for discussion.
The important principle is that the developer should be able to specify:

No Python execution
        OR
Component/client update
        OR
Fragment rerun
        OR
Full application rerun

This would complement Streamlit's existing progress toward selective reruns.

# 5. Shared Reactive State

Provide a lightweight mechanism for multiple components to observe the same application state without requiring a full application rerun for every update.
For example:

[python]
price = st.reactive_state("BTCUSDT.price")

chart.bind(price)
price_panel.bind(price)
order_panel.bind(price)

A state update could then propagate selectively:

             BTC price
                 │
       ┌─────────┼─────────┐
       ▼         ▼         ▼
     Chart     Metric    Order UI

This would be particularly useful for real-time applications where many UI elements depend on the same rapidly changing state.

The mechanism should ideally support:

* selective subscriptions
* batching
* throttling
* debouncing
* immutable snapshots
* explicit synchronization boundaries

# 6. High-Frequency Event Streams

Provide first-class support for event streams that may produce many updates per second.

Examples:

market ticks
sensor data
telemetry
mouse movement
chart crosshair
audio/video state
live logs
simulation output

Instead of:

event → rerun → render → event → rerun → render

the model could support:

event stream
     ↓
buffer / throttle / batch
     ↓
selected subscribers
     ↓
UI update

Developers should ideally be able to control:

[python]
throttle=50      # milliseconds
debounce=100
batch=True
max_rate=20

This would make realtime applications much easier to build while protecting the Python execution engine from excessive event traffic.

# 7. First-Class JavaScript / TypeScript Components

Streamlit's custom component architecture is extremely valuable, but highly interactive applications often require developers to move a significant amount of application logic into JavaScript/TypeScript.

A future component API could make this boundary more seamless.
Ideally, a component should be able to expose:

Python API
     │
     ├── persistent state
     ├── transient events
     ├── client-side actions
     └── server-side callbacks

without forcing developers to effectively build a separate frontend application.

For example:

[python]
chart = st.interactive_component(...)

chart.state
chart.events
chart.call("zoom_to", ...)
chart.emit("selection", ...)

The goal would be to make JavaScript/TypeScript an **extension of Streamlit**, rather than a parallel application architecture.

# 8. A Unified Event → State → Rerun Model

The eight ideas above could ultimately form one coherent programming model:

                 CLIENT
                   │
        ┌──────────┴──────────┐
        │                     │
      Events                State
        │                     │
        ▼                     ▼
   Event routing       State synchronization
        │                     │
        └──────────┬──────────┘
                   ▼
             Execution policy
                   │
        ┌──────────┼──────────┐
        ▼          ▼          ▼
      Client     Fragment     App
       only       rerun      rerun

This would preserve the simplicity that makes Streamlit attractive while giving developers much more control when building complex interactive applications.

# Example Use Case: Real-Time Trading Interface

A real-time trading terminal is a useful stress test for this model.
Consider a chart with draggable Entry, Stop Loss, and Take Profit levels.
During dragging:

Mouse movement
      ↓
Client-side chart update
      ↓
No Python rerun

When the user releases the mouse:

Drag end
      ↓
Event
      ↓
Python
      ↓
Risk calculation
      ↓
Order validation
      ↓
UI update

At the same time, market data could arrive independently:

WebSocket
    ↓
price event
    ↓
shared reactive state
    ↓
chart + position panel + P/L

This type of application currently requires a significant amount of custom frontend logic.

A more granular Streamlit event model could make such applications much more natural to implement while retaining Python as the primary application language.

# Why This Could Be Valuable Beyond Trading

The same architecture would benefit:

* real-time monitoring dashboards
* industrial control panels
* IoT interfaces
* scientific visualization
* financial terminals
* simulation environments
* visual editors
* workflow builders
* interactive maps
* multimedia applications
* operational dashboards
* collaborative applications

In other words, this would not be a trading-specific feature.

It would expand the category of applications that can be built naturally with Streamlit.

# Compatibility With the Existing Streamlit Model

This proposal does not require removing or fundamentally changing Streamlit's current execution model.

The existing model would remain the default:

Widget → Python → rerun

The new model would simply provide additional levels of control:

Client event
     ↓
   ┌───────────────────────────────┐
   │                               │
Client only → Fragment → App rerun


Developers building traditional data applications would not need to use any of this.

Developers building highly interactive applications could opt into it where necessary.

# Design Principle

The key principle could be summarized as:

> **Not every UI event should be a Python execution event.**

And similarly:

> **Not every state change needs to become a full application rerun.**

Streamlit has already been moving toward more granular execution and real-time interaction. A unified event/state model could provide the architectural layer that connects these improvements into a coherent system.

# Suggested Discussion Questions

Some questions that would be useful for the Streamlit team and community:

1. Should transient events and persistent component state be first-class, separate concepts?
2. Should client-only events be able to bypass Python entirely?
3. Should developers be able to explicitly select the rerun scope of an event?
4. Could shared reactive state be implemented without introducing a React-like programming model?
5. How should high-frequency events be throttled, debounced, or batched?
6. Could custom components expose a standardized event/state interface?
7. How far should Streamlit go toward supporting desktop-class interactive applications while retaining its Python-first simplicity?

---

## Conclusion

Streamlit's Python-first development model is one of its strongest advantages.

The goal should not be to turn Streamlit into React.

Instead, Streamlit could provide a **small, explicit event/state layer** that allows developers to build applications where:

* Python remains the application and business-logic layer;
* the browser handles high-frequency interaction locally;
* state can be synchronized selectively;
* events can be routed to client, fragment, or application scope;
* realtime streams can be throttled and batched;
* custom components can participate in the same model.

That would preserve Streamlit's simplicity while significantly expanding the class of interactive applications it can support.

For example, conceptually:

[python]
widget(
    on_change="client"
)

or:

[python]
widget(
    on_event="fragment"
)

or:

[python]
widget(
    on_event="app"
)

or:

[python]
widget(
    on_event="none"
)

The exact API is open for discussion.
The important principle is that the developer should be able to specify:

No Python execution
        OR
Component/client update
        OR
Fragment rerun
        OR
Full application rerun

This would complement Streamlit's existing progress toward selective reruns.

# 5. Shared Reactive State

Provide a lightweight mechanism for multiple components to observe the same application state without requiring a full application rerun for every update.
For example:

[python]
price = st.reactive_state("BTCUSDT.price")

chart.bind(price)
price_panel.bind(price)
order_panel.bind(price)

A state update could then propagate selectively:

             BTC price
                 │
       ┌─────────┼─────────┐
       ▼         ▼         ▼
     Chart     Metric    Order UI

This would be particularly useful for real-time applications where many UI elements depend on the same rapidly changing state.

The mechanism should ideally support:

* selective subscriptions
* batching
* throttling
* debouncing
* immutable snapshots
* explicit synchronization boundaries

# 6. High-Frequency Event Streams

Provide first-class support for event streams that may produce many updates per second.

Examples:

market ticks
sensor data
telemetry
mouse movement
chart crosshair
audio/video state
live logs
simulation output

Instead of:

event → rerun → render → event → rerun → render

the model could support:

event stream
     ↓
buffer / throttle / batch
     ↓
selected subscribers
     ↓
UI update

Developers should ideally be able to control:

[python]
throttle=50      # milliseconds
debounce=100
batch=True
max_rate=20

This would make realtime applications much easier to build while protecting the Python execution engine from excessive event traffic.

# 7. First-Class JavaScript / TypeScript Components

Streamlit's custom component architecture is extremely valuable, but highly interactive applications often require developers to move a significant amount of application logic into JavaScript/TypeScript.

A future component API could make this boundary more seamless.
Ideally, a component should be able to expose:

Python API
     │
     ├── persistent state
     ├── transient events
     ├── client-side actions
     └── server-side callbacks

without forcing developers to effectively build a separate frontend application.

For example:

[python]
chart = st.interactive_component(...)

chart.state
chart.events
chart.call("zoom_to", ...)
chart.emit("selection", ...)

The goal would be to make JavaScript/TypeScript an **extension of Streamlit**, rather than a parallel application architecture.

# 8. A Unified Event → State → Rerun Model

The eight ideas above could ultimately form one coherent programming model:

                 CLIENT
                   │
        ┌──────────┴──────────┐
        │                     │
      Events                State
        │                     │
        ▼                     ▼
   Event routing       State synchronization
        │                     │
        └──────────┬──────────┘
                   ▼
             Execution policy
                   │
        ┌──────────┼──────────┐
        ▼          ▼          ▼
      Client     Fragment     App
       only       rerun      rerun

This would preserve the simplicity that makes Streamlit attractive while giving developers much more control when building complex interactive applications.

# Example Use Case: Real-Time Trading Interface

A real-time trading terminal is a useful stress test for this model.
Consider a chart with draggable Entry, Stop Loss, and Take Profit levels.
During dragging:

Mouse movement
      ↓
Client-side chart update
      ↓
No Python rerun

When the user releases the mouse:

Drag end
      ↓
Event
      ↓
Python
      ↓
Risk calculation
      ↓
Order validation
      ↓
UI update

At the same time, market data could arrive independently:

WebSocket
    ↓
price event
    ↓
shared reactive state
    ↓
chart + position panel + P/L

This type of application currently requires a significant amount of custom frontend logic.

A more granular Streamlit event model could make such applications much more natural to implement while retaining Python as the primary application language.

# Why This Could Be Valuable Beyond Trading

The same architecture would benefit:

* real-time monitoring dashboards
* industrial control panels
* IoT interfaces
* scientific visualization
* financial terminals
* simulation environments
* visual editors
* workflow builders
* interactive maps
* multimedia applications
* operational dashboards
* collaborative applications

In other words, this would not be a trading-specific feature.

It would expand the category of applications that can be built naturally with Streamlit.

# Compatibility With the Existing Streamlit Model

This proposal does not require removing or fundamentally changing Streamlit's current execution model.

The existing model would remain the default:

Widget → Python → rerun

The new model would simply provide additional levels of control:

Client event
     ↓
   ┌───────────────────────────────┐
   │                               │
Client only → Fragment → App rerun


Developers building traditional data applications would not need to use any of this.

Developers building highly interactive applications could opt into it where necessary.

# Design Principle

The key principle could be summarized as:

> **Not every UI event should be a Python execution event.**

And similarly:

> **Not every state change needs to become a full application rerun.**

Streamlit has already been moving toward more granular execution and real-time interaction. A unified event/state model could provide the architectural layer that connects these improvements into a coherent system.

# Suggested Discussion Questions

Some questions that would be useful for the Streamlit team and community:

1. Should transient events and persistent component state be first-class, separate concepts?
2. Should client-only events be able to bypass Python entirely?
3. Should developers be able to explicitly select the rerun scope of an event?
4. Could shared reactive state be implemented without introducing a React-like programming model?
5. How should high-frequency events be throttled, debounced, or batched?
6. Could custom components expose a standardized event/state interface?
7. How far should Streamlit go toward supporting desktop-class interactive applications while retaining its Python-first simplicity?

---

## Conclusion

Streamlit's Python-first development model is one of its strongest advantages.

The goal should not be to turn Streamlit into React.

Instead, Streamlit could provide a **small, explicit event/state layer** that allows developers to build applications where:

* Python remains the application and business-logic layer;
* the browser handles high-frequency interaction locally;
* state can be synchronized selectively;
* events can be routed to client, fragment, or application scope;
* realtime streams can be throttled and batched;
* custom components can participate in the same model.

That would preserve Streamlit's simplicity while significantly expanding the class of interactive applications it can support.

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar issues.
- [x] I added a very descriptive title to this issue.
- [x] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue.

### Summary

When a launcher is started with `st.App(...).run()`, config options set through `STREAMLIT_*` environment variables (for example `STREAMLIT_SERVER_PORT` or `STREAMLIT_SERVER_FILE_WATCHER_TYPE`) have no effect, while the same launcher started with `streamlit run` honors them. The [`App.run()` docstring](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/blob/1.65.0/lib/streamlit/web/server/starlette/starlette_app.py#L543-L549) says that with `config=None`, "config comes from `config.toml` and environment variables as usual".

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
# page.py
import streamlit as st

st.write(st.get_option("server.port"))


# launcher.py
import streamlit as st

app = st.App("page.py")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run()
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Save the two files above next to each other.
2. Run `STREAMLIT_SERVER_PORT=8765 python launcher.py`.
3. Run `STREAMLIT_SERVER_PORT=8765 streamlit run launcher.py`.

### Expected Behavior

Both commands serve the app on port 8765.

### Current Behavior

- `python launcher.py` serves on the default port 8501, and the page shows `8501`.
- `streamlit run launcher.py` serves on 8765.

The same happens with other options. We hit it in production with `STREAMLIT_SERVER_FILE_WATCHER_TYPE=none`, `STREAMLIT_SERVER_RUN_ON_SAVE=false` and `STREAMLIT_CLIENT_SHOW_ERROR_DETAILS=type` set in our `Dockerfile`. All three were silently ignored, so the deployed app ran with file watching on and showed full error details.


### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.65.0
- Python version: 3.14.6
- Operating System: macOS 26 (Darwin 25.6.0), also reproduced on Linux in a container
- Browser: n/a

### Additional Information

The cause seems to be where environment variables are read:

- `config.get_config_options()` only applies environment variables for **sensitive** options (`_update_config_with_sensitive_env_var`).
- Every other option's environment variable reaches the config through the CLI: `streamlit.web.cli` uses click's `auto_envvar_prefix="STREAMLIT"` and per-option `envvar`, and click converts the values to the option types before they're passed to `bootstrap.load_config_options()`.
- `App.run()` calls `bootstrap.load_config_options(config_overrides)` directly, so it bypasses click, and those environment variables are never read.

Users can't easily work around this by passing `os.environ` values through `App.run(config=...)`, because `ConfigOption.set_value` doesn't convert them, so `"false"` stays a truthy string.

A possible fix is to have `App.run()` read the environment variable of each non-sensitive option, convert it the same way the CLI does, and apply it below the explicit `config=` overrides. Another option is to move environment variable handling into `get_config_options()` so every entry point gets it.

Our current workaround is to start the launcher through the CLI (`streamlit.web.cli.main(["run", "launcher.py"])`) and keep the module-level `app` object.

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar issues.
- [x] I added a very descriptive title to this issue.
- [x] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue.

### Summary

The element toolbar above an `st.dataframe` (Show/hide columns, Download as CSV, Search, Fullscreen) is in the Tab order, but `[data-testid="stElementToolbar"]` keeps `opacity: 0` while one of its buttons has keyboard focus. It only becomes visible on mouse hover. A keyboard user therefore tabs through four buttons they cannot see, which fails WCAG 2.4.7 (Focus Visible).

Related but distinct: #13332 (keyboard access to the column-header menu) and #17127 (toolbar target size, fixed).

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Add a `scope` parameter to `st.stop()`, mirroring `st.rerun(scope=...)`:

```python
st.stop(scope="app")       # default: current behaviour, halts the whole script run
st.stop(scope="fragment")  # halts only the currently executing fragment
```

With `scope="fragment"`, Streamlit would stop running the current fragment function. If the fragment is running as part of a full-app run, the rest of the script would continue from the statement after the fragment call.

### Why?

`st.stop()` is a common "guard clause" pattern: check a precondition, show a message, stop. Inside a fragment, though, `st.stop()` stops the *entire* script run when the fragment executes during a full-app run. Everything rendered after the fragment call is skipped, even though only the fragment's own precondition failed.
It would be useful when you have a called child function in the fragment that has st.stop in with its own conditions that you'd want to stop the flow of the parent.

Example:

```python
import streamlit as st

def some_stop_condition():
     now = datetime.now()
     if now < datetime.combine(now.date(), time(16, 45)):
           st.warning("You can't use this service before 4:45pm")
           st.stop(scope="fragment")

@st.fragment
def upload_panel():
    some_stop_condition()
    file = st.file_uploader("Upload a CSV")
    if file is None:
        st.info("Upload a file to see a preview.")
        st.stop()  # intent: stop this panel only
    st.dataframe(load(file))

st.title("Dashboard")
upload_panel()
st.header("Other section")  # skipped on full-app runs when no file is uploaded
render_other_stuff()
```

The usual workaround is `return`, but that only works at the top level of the fragment function. When the guard lives in a helper called from the fragment, you have to thread return values or flags back up through every layer, or raise and catch a custom exception. `st.stop(scope="fragment")` would give fragments the same clean early-exit that `st.stop()` gives scripts.

This also fits with the existing API. Since `st.rerun` already supports `scope="fragment"`, users reasonably expect the same option on `st.stop`. It would also be useful inside `@st.dialog` functions, which are built on fragments.

### How?

### Summary

Provide a managed API for starting one-shot background work in response to an explicit signal, such as a button click or form submission.

Unlike background cache refresh, each start is an intentional action and the result should not be memoized.

```python
task = st.task(key="generate_report")

if st.button("Generate report"):
    task.start(generate_report, uploaded_data)

if task.running:
    st.info("Generating report...")
elif task.done:
    st.download_button("Download report", task.result)
elif task.error:
    st.error(task.error)
```

### Why?

Some work should:

- start only after an explicit user action;
- continue without blocking the app;
- survive script reruns;
- expose its running, completed, and error states; and
- execute exactly once per explicit start.

Examples include generating a report, sending an email, writing to a database, triggering a pipeline, or running an LLM request.

### Related

- #6687 — broader background execution request, closed after the cached-computation pattern became available
- #10578 — work interrupted by reruns
- #14524 — rerun-resilient UI streaming, a distinct use case

### Summary

Example 3: Update a toast message on the st.toast documentation page fails. The first toast shows but does not update. Regression came about in 1.59 as part of #15523. Also related to #16498.

### Reproducible Code Example

```Python
import time
import streamlit as st

def cook_breakfast():
    msg = st.toast("Gathering ingredients...")
    time.sleep(1)
    msg.toast("Cooking...")
    time.sleep(1)
    msg.toast("Ready!", icon="🥞")

if st.button("Cook breakfast"):
    cook_breakfast()
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Run the code
2. Click the button
3. Watch as the toast does not update

### Expected Behavior

Watch as the toast updates to reflect the new message.

### Current Behavior

No error message in either the python or in the browser console. 

### Is this a regression?

- [x] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.66
- Python version: 3.15
- Operating System: 15.8.1 (24H32)
- Browser: Firefox and Chrome

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Add a `streamlit deploy` CLI command for headless, non-interactive deployment and updates of Streamlit apps directly from the terminal. Ideally, it works out of the box with **Streamlit Community Cloud**, **Streamlit in Snowflake (SiS)**, and at least one external cloud target (e.g. **Cloudflare**), and provides a way to inspect server logs (e.g. `streamlit deploy --logs`).

### Why?

AI coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, etc.) can already scaffold, run (`streamlit run`), and test Streamlit apps locally, but there is no unified, headless way for an agent to **deploy an app, push updates, and read remote server logs** to verify the deployment or debug startup crashes.

Today, deploying requires browser-based flows (Community Cloud), separate ecosystem CLIs with their own project layouts (`snow streamlit deploy`, `wrangler`, etc.), or manual container setups. A built-in, agent-friendly `streamlit deploy` command closes the loop from local authoring to a live shareable URL.

### How?

Introduce a `streamlit deploy` CLI command modeled after `streamlit run`:

```bash
# Deploy or update an app (uses detected/configured target)
streamlit deploy streamlit_app.py

# Explicitly select a deployment target
streamlit deploy streamlit_app.py --target community-cloud
streamlit deploy streamlit_app.py --target snowflake
streamlit deploy streamlit_app.py --target cloudflare

# Inspect or stream server logs of the deployed app
streamlit deploy --logs
```

Key capabilities & design patterns:

- **Out-of-the-box targets (pluggable provider model):**
  - **Streamlit Community Cloud** (e.g. via GitHub repo coordinates / API or direct bundle upload).
  - **Streamlit in Snowflake (SiS)** (e.g. delegating to `snowflake-cli` / `snow streamlit` or native connection config).
  - **External provider (e.g. Cloudflare Workers / Containers)** for quick standalone hosting (potentially building on `streamlit dockerize`, #16307).
- **Idempotent create-or-update with persisted project state:**
  - Persist non-secret deployment metadata (target provider, app ID/slug, entrypoint, deployed URL) in the project (e.g. `.streamlit/deploy.toml` or `config.toml`) so subsequent `streamlit deploy` and `streamlit deploy --logs` calls work with zero arguments.
- **Server log access & closed-loop verification:**
  - Support fetching/streaming build and runtime logs (e.g. `streamlit deploy --logs [--follow]` or `streamlit deploy logs`).
  - Automatically surface startup errors / tracebacks and exit non-zero if the deployed app fails its initial health check or boot run, so agents can self-correct.
- **Headless & agent-friendly UX:**
  - Non-interactive execution (`--yes` / env var / token auth) with a one-time login flow (`streamlit deploy --login` or reusing `gh` / `snow` / `wrangler` credentials).
  - Structured output option (`--json`) returning the deployed URL, status, and app identifier.
  - Sync `.streamlit/secrets.toml` / environment variables safely when requested (e.g. `--secrets`).

### Additional Context

- Related:
  - #13635 — Allow Cursor or other AI agents to deploy to Community Cloud
  - #16307 — Add a `streamlit dockerize` CLI command to package an app into a Docker image
  - [PR #16843 — Agent-app interface spec](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/16843)

### Summary

Add a `streamlit deploy` CLI command for headless, non-interactive deployment and updates of Streamlit apps directly from the terminal. Ideally, it works out of the box with **Streamlit Community Cloud**, **Streamlit in Snowflake (SiS)**, and at least one external cloud target (e.g. **Cloudflare**), and provides a way to inspect server logs (e.g. `streamlit deploy --logs`).

### Why?

AI coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, etc.) can already scaffold, run (`streamlit run`), and test Streamlit apps locally, but there is no unified, headless way for an agent to **deploy an app, push updates, and read remote server logs** to verify the deployment or debug startup crashes.

Today, deploying requires browser-based flows (Community Cloud), separate ecosystem CLIs with their own project layouts (`snow streamlit deploy`, `wrangler`, etc.), or manual container setups. A built-in, agent-friendly `streamlit deploy` command closes the loop from local authoring to a live shareable URL.

### How?

Introduce a `streamlit deploy` CLI command modeled after `streamlit run`:

```bash
# Deploy or update an app (uses detected/configured target)
streamlit deploy streamlit_app.py

# Explicitly select a deployment target
streamlit deploy streamlit_app.py --target community-cloud
streamlit deploy streamlit_app.py --target snowflake
streamlit deploy streamlit_app.py --target cloudflare

# Inspect or stream server logs of the deployed app
streamlit deploy --logs
```

Key capabilities & design patterns:

- **Out-of-the-box targets (pluggable provider model):**
  - **Streamlit Community Cloud** (e.g. via GitHub repo coordinates / API or direct bundle upload).
  - **Streamlit in Snowflake (SiS)** (e.g. delegating to `snowflake-cli` / `snow streamlit` or native connection config).
  - **External provider (e.g. Cloudflare Workers / Containers)** for quick standalone hosting (potentially building on `streamlit dockerize`, #16307).
- **Idempotent create-or-update with persisted project state:**
  - Persist non-secret deployment metadata (target provider, app ID/slug, entrypoint, deployed URL) in the project (e.g. `.streamlit/deploy.toml` or `config.toml`) so subsequent `streamlit deploy` and `streamlit deploy --logs` calls work with zero arguments.
- **Server log access & closed-loop verification:**
  - Support fetching/streaming build and runtime logs (e.g. `streamlit deploy --logs [--follow]` or `streamlit deploy logs`).
  - Automatically surface startup errors / tracebacks and exit non-zero if the deployed app fails its initial health check or boot run, so agents can self-correct.
- **Headless & agent-friendly UX:**
  - Non-interactive execution (`--yes` / env var / token auth) with a one-time login flow (`streamlit deploy --login` or reusing `gh` / `snow` / `wrangler` credentials).
  - Structured output option (`--json`) returning the deployed URL, status, and app identifier.
  - Sync `.streamlit/secrets.toml` / environment variables safely when requested (e.g. `--secrets`).

### Additional Context

Retract Go module `github.com/stretchrcom/testify` which is visible on `pkg.go.dev` (I'm not linking here on purpose) with releases `v1.1.1` to `v1.2.2`.

## What happened?

The `stretch` GitHub organization was at some point in history named `stretchrcom`. As a result, the Testify repository is also accessible via a redirect from that organization. And Google seems to have fetch the repository under the `github.com/stretchrcom/testify` and it is currently (2026-05-15) visible at `https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/stretchrcom/testify` with releases `v1.1.1` to `v1.2.2`. New releases stopped to appear with that path when `go.mod` has been added in c45a1382af909f3ed0abc3b8d8e59e6db48ed9d8 published from release `v1.3.0`.

## What to do?

The official package path has always been `github.com/stretchr/testify`. Nobody has ever imported this project under `github.com/stretchrcom/testify`. So it makes no sense to have `github.com/stretchrcom/testify` visible on `pkg.go.dev`.

So let's clean this invalid alternate module.

`AssertNumberOfCalls` currently calls `m.calls()`, which copies the entire call history before counting entries with a matching method name. The method already holds `m.mutex` throughout the loop, and the loop only reads `call.Method`.

The copy originally served a purpose. In [b11fb16](https://github.com/stretchr/testify/commit/b11fb1691542b198b0c1c2156b97a661f8b9c2d6), `calls()` acquired the mutex, copied the slice, and released the mutex before the caller iterated over it. Later, [bd79c01](https://github.com/stretchr/testify/commit/bd79c01e742b23500fc1d7c40880506473831597) moved locking into `AssertNumberOfCalls` and removed the lock inside `calls()`, but kept the copy.

Could this particular loop iterate over `m.Calls` directly?

```diff
- for _, call := range m.calls() {
+ for _, call := range m.Calls {
```

I benchmarked this against commit `435c07b5`, repeatedly checking 100 recorded calls with a minimal test reporter. On Ubuntu 24.04 ARM64 in Lima, using Go 1.27.1, the median of 10 runs changed as follows:

- Time per assertion: 3.60 µs to 0.447 µs.
- Bytes allocated per assertion: 18,564 to 128.
- Allocations per assertion: 4 to 3.

This measures the assertion itself. An empty history showed no clear improvement: about 177 ns before and 179 ns after on recheck, with unchanged allocations.

The lock, counting logic, and failure message would remain unchanged. The local prototype passed the full test suite and race checks on macOS and Linux. This proposal only covers `AssertNumberOfCalls`, leaving `calls()` and its other callers unchanged.

## `Eventually` / `Never` panic instead of failing, and a nil `condition` takes the whole binary down

These assertions are supposed to report a failure through the `TestingT` they are given.
Four of them do not: with a `nil` condition, or a `tick` that is zero or negative, they
panic. The nil case is the worse of the two, because the panic happens on a goroutine
`Eventually` spawns, so the caller cannot recover it and `t.Errorf` is never reached.

```go
package main

import (
	"testing"
	"time"

	"github.com/stretchr/testify/assert"
)

func TestNothing(t *testing.T) {
	assert.Eventually(t, nil, 10*time.Millisecond, time.Millisecond)
}
```

```
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
[signal SIGSEGV: segmentation violation code=0x1 addr=0x0 pc=0x0]

goroutine 1 [running]:
github.com/stretchr/testify/assert.Eventually.func1()
	assert/assertions.go:2013
created by github.com/stretchr/testify/assert.Eventually in goroutine 1
```

`recover()` in the test cannot catch that, so one nil slips into a helper and the entire
test binary aborts with a stack trace pointing into testify, rather than one test failing
with a message.

The cause is two lines:

```go
// assert/assertions.go:2012-2024
ch := make(chan bool, 1)
checkCond := func() { ch <- condition() }
...
go checkCond()
```

`condition` is dereferenced on the goroutine with no nil check, and `tick` goes straight
into `time.NewTicker`, which panics on a non-positive interval.

<details>
<summary>All eight paths, each reproduced in its own process</summary>

| call | result |
|---|---|
| `assert.Eventually(t, nil, d, d)` | panic, goroutine 1, binary aborts |
| `assert.Never(t, nil, d, d)` | panic, goroutine 19 |
| `assert.EventuallyWithT(t, nil, d, d)` | panic, goroutine 19 |
| `assert.NeverWithT(t, nil, d, d)` | panic, goroutine 19 |
| `assert.Eventually(t, cond, time.Second, 0)` | `panic: non-positive interval for NewTicker` |
| `assert.Never(t, cond, time.Second, 0)` | same |
| `assert.Eventually(t, cond, time.Second, -time.Second)` | same |

The `tick` ones are less severe — a `recover()` in the caller does catch those, and a
caller who passes `0` has arguably written a mistake — but they are still a panic where a
message would do, and `tick=0` is easy to reach by computing the interval.
</details>

## A nil guard for this already exists in the same file

`isFunction` gets it right, which is why `assert.Equal(t, nil, someFunc)` reports a failure
instead of crashing:

```go
// assert/assertions.go:1974
func isFunction(arg interface{}) bool {
	if arg == nil {
		return false
	}
	return reflect.TypeOf(arg).Kind() == reflect.Func
}
```

## Not re-raising the `Subset` part, but asking about the rest of that family

While sweeping the assertion surface I hit the same shape in eight more assertions, all
from one unguarded `reflect.TypeOf(x).Kind()` — `reflect.TypeOf(nil)` is nil, so `.Kind()`
dereferences it:

| site | assertions affected |
|---|---|
| `assert/assertions.go:1016`, `:1084` | `Subset`, `NotSubset` |
| `assert/assertions.go:1163` (`isList`) | `ElementsMatch`, `NotElementsMatch` |
| `assert/assertion_order.go:10` (`isOrdered`) | `IsIncreasing`, `IsNonIncreasing`, `IsDecreasing`, `IsNonDecreasing` |

So `assert.IsIncreasing(t, nil)`, `assert.ElementsMatch(t, nil, []int{1})` and
`assert.Subset(t, nil, []int{1})` all panic with the same nil dereference.

`Subset` and `NotSubset` were reported before, in #1918, closed on 2026-07-29 without a
comment, so I am deliberately **not** re-filing that part — I would rather ask than
re-litigate. I cannot tell whether that close was about those two functions or about the
approach, so: is a nil guard welcome for the other six, or is passing nil a caller error
across the board? If the latter, a `panic` with a clear message may be the more honest
outcome than a failure report, and I will drop it.

There is one more in the same family, which is not a `reflect` issue:
`matchRegexp` type-asserts and then dereferences, so a typed nil slips past:

```go
// assert/assertions.go:1711
if rr, ok := rx.(*regexp.Regexp); ok {
	r = rr
}
...
return r.MatchString(v)   // r is nil here
```

`assert.Regexp(t, (*regexp.Regexp)(nil), "x")` panics. A malformed pattern also panics,
via `regexp.MustCompile`, but that one I read as idiomatic for a caller error — and it is
already being dealt with in #1857 — so I am only raising the typed-nil case.

## What I would send

Happy to open a PR for the `Eventually` family and `matchRegexp` — a nil check on
`condition`, a `tick <= 0` check that fails with a message, and a `rx == nil` check — with
tests for each. I have not touched the `reflect` family pending your answer above.

Reproduced against `master` at `87a7b9d` with Go 1.24.3.

### Describe the bug

I found a behaviour regarding `store.subscribe()` that doesn't match between v5 and v4

```ts
value.subscribe((newValue) => console.log(newValue, $value));
```

In the callback, the given parameter `newValue` is up to date while the $ accessor `$value` is not in v5. The both used to be updated in v4

Not sure if it's an intentional breaking change. I understand it wouldn't be a good idea to mix up using both `newValue` and `$value` anyway

### Reproduction

Here is the code:

```svelte
<script>
	import { writable } from 'svelte/store';

	const value = writable(100);
	value.subscribe((newValue) => console.log(newValue, $value));
</script>

<input bind:value={$value} type="number" />
```

- v5: https://svelte.dev/playground/01ab0d2cb45149f1b2db645c0cbed251?version=5.47.1
- v4: https://svelte.dev/playground/01ab0d2cb45149f1b2db645c0cbed251?version=4.2.20


### Logs

```shell
When I change the input from 100 to 101:

- v5 shows "101, 100"
- v4 shows "101, 101"
```

this maybe
```svelte
<script>

```svelte
<script>
let { className = $className() } = $props()
</script>

<button class={className}>SWAAAAG</button>
````

### Alternatives considered

or maybe just dont nuke these styles if class is used inside that component???? I think it sounds even better that whatever i wrote above

nice to have

### Describe the problem

4 months ago, a change #16636 was made to default the css hash id from being based on the contents of the style block itself to filenames.  

The rationale was that it was better to keep the hashes more consistent across deployments, however it breaks the uniqueness in an MFE situation.  If multiple Svelte runtimes are loaded in the same page which happen to declare styles in components of the same filename, there is a collision and the first loaded is the only style that is injected.

I am aware it is possible to override the cssHash function, but it is a subtle issue that in my opinion would be better served with different defaulting behavior

### Describe the proposed solution

I do not know what would be a good solution, but two options that come to mind would be:
1. Revert the change and default back to the style tag contents.  
2. Introduce an application level identifier (package name maybe?) to be combined with the filename when hashing to scope it to the specific application

### Importance

would make my life easier

{/each} ``` **App.svelte** ```svelte ``` ### Severity annoyance

### Describe the bug

This is related to #17762 .

Looking back it should've been obvious... since the static analyzer no longer sees the `import()` call, esbuild no longer resolves it in `--bundle` mode ([docs](https://esbuild.github.io/api/#bundle)), so the resulting source code looks like this:

```js
var obfuscated_import = (module_name) => import(
  /* @vite-ignore */
  module_name
);
```

There's obviously no error at build time, it just hits you at runtime when running the `.cjs` file because... well, esbuild is supposed to resolve the `import()`, but it's not, and a cjs only runtime has no idea what `import()` is.

I honestly don't know if this is fixable unless `node:crypto` is dropped, aka node 18 is dropped.

Another alternative would be to use a userland crypto package instead of something from the platform, but I don't know if that's doable or even worth it, this is getting ridiculous.

I'll come up with some patch-work on my end, I'll probably have to straight up remove that code from the bundle and cross my fingers.

I'm just opening this because I thought I should let you guys know about the issue.

### Reproduction

Full reproduction can be found here https://github.com/razshare/svelte-reproduction-issue-17771
