### Describe the bug

If `tauri.conf.json` is saved with a UTF-8 byte order mark (`EF BB BF`), Tauri fails to
parse it and reports a generic JSON syntax error pointing at line 1, column 1. The file is
valid JSON and looks completely correct in an editor, so the actual cause (an invisible
leading byte) is not discoverable from the error message.

This is easy to hit on Windows, because PowerShell — the default shell — writes a BOM for
several common encoding options. Any script or tooling that regenerates or rewrites the
config can silently introduce it.

### Reproduction

1. Create a Tauri v2 app.
2. Rewrite the config with PowerShell, which prepends a BOM:
   ```powershell
   $c = Get-Content tauri.conf.json -Raw
   Set-Content tauri.conf.json -Value $c -Encoding UTF8
   ```
3. Verify the BOM is present:
   ```
   $ xxd tauri.conf.json | head -1
   00000000: efbb bf7b 0a20 2022 2473 6368 656d 6122  ...{.  "$schema"
   ```
4. Run any command that loads the config (e.g. `cargo tauri build`).

### Expected behavior

The config is parsed normally. A UTF-8 BOM is a legal way to encode a UTF-8 file, and most
JSON consumers either skip it or say explicitly that it is the problem.

### Actual behavior

Parsing fails with a `serde_json` syntax error at line 1 column 1. Nothing in the message
mentions a BOM or an encoding issue, and the file renders as valid JSON in every editor,
so the failure looks like config corruption rather than an encoding problem.

### Root cause

In `tauri-utils` (2.9.3), `src/config/parse.rs`:

- `:282` — `let raw = read_to_string(&path)?;` — this wraps `std::fs::read_to_string`
  (`:393`), which validates UTF-8 but does **not** strip a BOM: `U+FEFF` is valid UTF-8 and
  is kept in the returned `String`.
- `:351-355` — `do_parse_json` passes `raw` straight to `serde_json::from_str` with no
  normalization:
  ```rust
  fn do_parse_json<D: DeserializeOwned>(raw: &str, path: &Path) -> Result<D, ConfigError> {
    serde_json::from_str(raw).map_err(|error| ConfigError::FormatJson {
      path: path.into(),
      error,
    })
  }
  ```
- `serde_json` rejects the leading `U+FEFF` and reports `expected value at line 1 column 1`.

Note that when the `config-json5` feature is enabled, `:288-300` tries JSON5 first and, on
failure, falls back to reporting the `serde_json` error — so the surfaced message is the
same either way. The comment there already anticipates that this can be confusing.

### Suggested fix

Strip a leading BOM once, right after the file is read, so every format path benefits:

```rust
let raw = read_to_string(&path)?;
let raw = raw.strip_prefix('\u{feff}').unwrap_or(&raw).to_string();
```

Alternatively, do it inside the `read_to_string` helper at `:393`, which also covers the
`.json5` (`:306`) and `.toml` (`:318`) branches.

If stripping is not desirable, detecting the BOM and returning a dedicated error that names
it would at least make the failure diagnosable.

### Platform and versions

- OS: Windows 11 (also reproducible anywhere a BOM-prefixed config is produced)
- Tauri: v2 (`tauri = "2"`, `tauri-build = "2"`)
- `tauri-utils`: 2.9.3
- Config schema: `https://schema.tauri.app/config/2`

### Prior art

`serde_json` deliberately does not skip BOMs, so consumers are expected to handle it. Other
tools in this space normalize it at the read boundary for exactly this reason. #15601 notes
a related BOM pitfall elsewhere in the Tauri toolchain (`latest.json` must be written
BOM-free), which suggests handling this once at the config read boundary would remove a
recurring class of confusing failures.

I'm happy to open a PR with the fix above if you'd like.

WeType), which should emit the full-width colon `：`, produces nothing. Pressing
it a second time emits the character. This happens every time — not once per
window, not once per session.

The built-in "Pinyin – Simplified" input method is unaffected in the same app,
in the same field.

### The part that narrows it down

Safari on the same machine, on the same page, with the same input method, is
**not** affected. Safari is also WebKit, so this does not look like a WKWebView
text-input bug — the difference is the hosting window/view, which points at tao
or wry rather than WebKit itself. Feel free to transfer this issue if that is
where it belongs.

### What I ruled out before filing

- **Our own JavaScript.** Every `keydown` listener in the app was audited. Only
  `Escape`, `Tab` and `Enter` are handled, and the `Enter` path is already
  IME-aware (`isComposing` plus the legacy `keyCode === 229` fallback). Nothing
  calls `preventDefault` on the key in question.
- **Injected scripts.** The app's `initialization_script` contains no key
  handling at all.
- **AppKit work the app does.** A titlebar accessory view controller (secondary
  windows only) and `NSNotificationCenter` observers for fullscreen transitions.
  Neither touches the responder chain of the main window's content view.
- **Secure Input.** Not enabled — verified with
  `ioreg -l -w 0 | grep SecureInput` while the app was running and focused. This
  was the strongest candidate, since Secure Input blocks third-party IMEs while
  leaving Apple's own ones working, but it is off.

2. Open any Tauri app with a text input in the WebView.

## Describe the problem

A plugin author cannot get a value set on their own Rust `Builder` into their Android or iOS plugin. The only configuration a native plugin receives comes from the app's `tauri.conf.json`.

`Plugin::initialize` builds the `PluginApi` from the config Tauri read out of `plugins.<name>`, and `register_android_plugin` / `register_ios_plugin` forward that same `raw_config` to the native `load()`:

```rust
// tauri/src/plugin.rs:799
raw_config: Arc::new(config.clone()),

// tauri/src/plugin/mobile.rs:172 and :262
let config = self.raw_config.clone();
```

`raw_config` is private, only ever assigned in `initialize`, and `plugin::Builder` exposes no method to contribute to it. The path is closed by construction.

This matters because a Rust builder is the idiomatic way to configure a Tauri plugin — `tauri-plugin-log`, `tauri-plugin-updater`, `tauri-plugin-store` and `tauri-plugin-window-state` all use one — but the pattern stops working the moment a plugin has a native mobile implementation. And `tauri.conf.json` can only hold a literal, so a value like `concat!("my-app/", env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION"))`, or one read from an environment variable or a Cargo feature, cannot be expressed there at all.

It looks like nobody has solved this so much as avoided it: across `plugins-workspace`, `opener` is the only plugin with both a plugin-owned Rust `Builder` and a native mobile layer, and its builder field never crosses the bridge.

## Describe the solution you'd like

Additive methods on `PluginApi` that take the config at the registration call site:

```rust
let handle = api.register_android_plugin_with_config(
   "org.example.plugin", "ExamplePlugin",
   serde_json::json!({ "userAgent": user_agent }),
)?;
```

- **No native-side change.** Android's `Plugin.getConfig(Class)` and Swift's `parseConfig(_:)` already consume this exact JSON string.
- **No merge policy to invent.** A `Builder::default_config()` merged with `tauri.conf.json` raises questions with no obviously right answer — which side wins, and is the merge deep or shallow. At the registration site the author already has `api.config()` in scope and can merge however the plugin wants.
- **Purely additive.** Existing `register_*_plugin` behaviour is unchanged.

A `Builder::mobile_config(impl Serialize)` populating `raw_config` before registration would work too, and reads better at the definition site. Either is fine; merge semantics are the only reason to prefer the explicit one.

## Alternatives considered

**Push the value with a plugin command after registration** — the current workaround. Define a native `configure` command and invoke it from `setup()` right after `register_*_plugin`, via `run_mobile_plugin`.

It works, and the ordering is safe: registration blocks until the native plugin is loaded, and `setup()` runs before the event loop exists, so it lands before the webview can invoke anything. `run_mobile_plugin` also bypasses the ACL, so the command needs no `build.rs` `COMMANDS` entry or permission and stays unreachable from JS. The costs:

- The same boilerplate command in Kotlin **and** Swift for every plugin that needs it.
- A failed push propagates out of `setup()`, aborting plugin initialisation — and with the `.expect(...)` every documented bootstrap uses, panicking the app at launch. That is harsh for what may be a cosmetic setting, with nowhere obvious to degrade gracefully.
- It is undiscoverable. Nothing in the plugin-development docs suggests it and no official plugin demonstrates it, so each author rediscovers the limitation from the Tauri source and reinvents the same fix.

**Require `tauri.conf.json`** — what the ecosystem does today. Rules out computed values, and splits a plugin's configuration across two places when it also has Rust-side options.

**Keep the implementation in Rust and skip the native plugin** — how `tauri-plugin-http` sidesteps the problem entirely, with no `android/` or `ios/` directory. Not available to plugins that exist precisely because they need platform APIs.

body_text:
### Describe the bug

On Windows, `tauri dev` starts `beforeDevCommand` as a plain `cmd /S /C "<script>"` child through `std::process::Command` and keeps no OS-level coupling to it: no job object, no process group. The only code that tears that tree down is `kill_before_dev_process()` (the PowerShell `Kill-Tree`), and it is reachable only from the `ctrlc` console handler and from the CLI's own normal exit paths (`on_app_exit`, the error return of `dev::command`).

So whenever the CLI process ends any other way — `taskkill /F /PID <cli>` without `/T`, `Stop-Process`, Task Manager "End task", `process.kill(pid)` from a Node wrapper, or simply being the direct child of a Node process that exits (libuv puts direct children in a kill-on-close job and terminates them silently) — the whole `cmd /S /C "npm run dev"` → `npm` → `cmd /d /s /c vite` → `node vite.js` → `esbuild` tree survives with a dead parent. Vite keeps `[::1]:1420` and the next `tauri dev` fails with `Port 1420 is already in use`. The frontend never notices the CLI is gone: there is no SIGTERM on Windows, and Vite's `process.stdin.on('end', …)` guard never fires because a non-TTY stdin is never read (`'end'` only fires on a stream that is being consumed).

### Reproduction

Any Vite project — `create-tauri-app` defaults (`beforeDevCommand: "npm run dev"`, `devUrl: "http://localhost:1420"`) are enough.

1. In a terminal: `node node_modules\@tauri-apps\cli\tauri.js dev` (or `npm run tauri dev`; the process to look at is the `node.exe … tauri.js dev` one, which is the CLI).
2. Wait for `VITE … ready`. `netstat -ano | findstr :1420` shows `LISTENING <vite pid>`.
3. Terminate **only** the CLI process: `taskkill /F /PID <pid of node tauri.js>` (no `/T`), or `Stop-Process -Id <pid> -Force`.
4. `netstat -ano | findstr :1420` → still `LISTENING`, same PID. `tasklist` / `Get-CimInstance Win32_Process` still show `cmd /S /C "npm run dev"` → `npm-cli.js run dev` → `cmd /d /s /c vite` → `node vite.js`, with the parent PID pointing at the dead CLI. Run `tauri dev` again → `Port 1420 is already in use`.

Same outcome when the CLI is the direct child of a Node script (`spawn(process.execPath, ['node_modules/@tauri-apps/cli/tauri.js', 'dev'])`) and that script is terminated: libuv's per-process job kills the CLI at once (exit code 0, nothing logged), and everything the CLI spawned through `std::process` is outside that job (`JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_SILENT_BREAKAWAY_OK`) and stays.

Captured on Windows Server 2022 10.0.20348, node 26.7.0, `@tauri-apps/cli` 2.11.4, vite 7.3.6 (timestamps from a script that polls `Get-Process` / `Get-NetTCPConnection` every second; the CLI was launched from `cmd /d /s /c` in its own console, no Node wrapper):

```
[23:30:13] BEFORE: process tree
cmd.exe PID=8936   /d /s /c "node node_modules\@tauri-apps\cli\tauri.js dev …"
  node.exe PID=9972   tauri.js dev …                                   <- the CLI
    cmd.exe PID=10096   "cmd" /S /C "npm run dev"                     <- beforeDevCommand
      node.exe PID=4116   npm-cli.js run dev
        cmd.exe PID=8724   /d /s /c vite
          node.exe PID=9308   vite.js                                 <- LISTENING [::1]:1420
            esbuild.exe PID=9220   --service=0.28.1 --ping
    cargo.exe PID=4964   cargo run --no-default-features --color always --
      cargo.exe PID=1908 -> rustc.exe PID=3052
  port 1420: ::1:1420 Listen PID=9308

[23:30:14] taskkill /F /PID 9972        (the CLI only; no /T)  -> exit 0
t+ 1s  cli=False  beforeDev-cmd=True  vite=True  cargo=True  listen1420=PID 9308
t+ 5s  cli=False  beforeDev-cmd=True  vite=True  cargo=True  listen1420=PID 9308
t+15s  cli=False  beforeDev-cmd=True  vite=True  cargo=True  listen1420=PID 9308

[23:30:31] AFTER 15s: surviving tree, root cmd PID=10096 (its parent 9972 alive=False)
cmd.exe PID=10096 PPID=9972   "cmd" /S /C "npm run dev"
  node.exe PID=4116           npm-cli.js run dev
    cmd.exe PID=8724          /d /s /c vite
      node.exe PID=9308       vite.js
        esbuild.exe PID=9220
  port 1420: ::1:1420 Listen PID=9308
CLI log: 927 bytes before, 927 bytes after — nothing written, no cleanup ran.
cleanup: taskkill /T /F /PID 10096 -> all five terminated; port 1420 free.
```

Second capture, same machine and versions, CLI launched as the direct child of a Node script (`spawn(process.execPath, [tauri.js, 'dev', …])`) and that script terminated with `Stop-Process -Force`:

```
t+0.06s  PID 8868   node (the wrapper script)   EXITED 0xFFFFFFFF
t+0.06s  PID 10128  node tauri.js dev           EXITED 0x00000000   <- killed by libuv's job, nothing logged
after 15s  cmd "cmd" /S /C "npm run dev" -> npm -> cmd vite -> node vite.js (PID 9536)  STILL ALIVE, LISTENING [::1]:1420
after 15s  cargo -> cargo -> app                STILL ALIVE (this half collapses on its own when the app exits; Vite never does)
```

Control: `taskkill /T /F` on the tree root kills everything and nothing leaks — the tree itself is fine, the CLI just never gets a chance to run `Kill-Tree`.

### Expected behavior

The `beforeDevCommand` tree should end with the CLI regardless of *how* the CLI ends — the way `cargo` already couples its children to itself on Windows. Putting the spawned `cmd` into a job object created with `JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE` right after `SharedChild::spawn` (`CreateJobObjectW` + `SetInformationJobObject` + `AssignProcessToJobObject`, keeping the handle for the CLI's lifetime) makes the OS tear the tree down on any exit, `TerminateProcess` included; nested jobs work on Windows 8 / Server 2012 and later, so this also holds when the CLI itself runs inside npm's or libuv's job. `kill_before_dev_process` would still cover the graceful Ctrl-C path.

### Full `tauri info` output

```text
[✔] Environment
    - OS: Windows 10.0.20348 x86_64 (X64)
    ✔ WebView2: 151.0.4129.107
    ✔ MSVC: Visual Studio Build Tools 2022
    ✔ rustc: 1.97.1 (8bab26f4f 2026-07-14)
    ✔ cargo: 1.97.1 (c980f4866 2026-06-30)
    ✔ rustup: 1.27.1 (54dd3d00f 2024-04-24)
    ✔ Rust toolchain: 1.97.1-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc (overridden by rust-toolchain.toml)
    - node: 26.7.0
    - npm: 11.19.0

[-] Packages
    - tauri 🦀: 2.11.5
    - tauri-build 🦀: 2.6.3
    - wry 🦀: 0.55.1, (outdated, latest: 0.56.1)
    - tao 🦀: 0.35.3, (outdated, latest: 0.37.0)
    - @tauri-apps/api  ⱼₛ: 2.11.1
    - @tauri-apps/cli  ⱼₛ: 2.11.4

[-] App
    - build-type: bundle
    - frontendDist: ../dist
    - devUrl: http://localhost:1420/
    - framework: React
    - bundler: Vite
```

### Stack trace

_No response_ — nothing is logged; the CLI is gone before it could.

### Additional context

Where this is in `crates/tauri-cli/src/dev.rs` at `@tauri-apps/cli-v2.11.4` (the file is byte-identical on `dev` @ dd6befda, 2026-08-26):

- L166–170: `Command::new("cmd").arg("/S").arg("/C").arg(&before_dev)` — no creation flags, no job.
- L206–209: `SharedChild::spawn`, stored in the `BEFORE_DEV` static; L220–223: `ctrlc::set_handler(|| { kill_before_dev_process(); exit(130) })`.
- L102–105 (`command` error path) and L322–330 (`on_app_exit`) are the only other callers of `kill_before_dev_process`.
- L332–370: the Windows cleanup is `powershell -NoProfile -Command "function Kill-Tree {…}; Kill-Tree <pid>"` followed by `child.kill()` — it runs inside the CLI's own process, so it cannot run after a `TerminateProcess`.
- The shipped `cli.win32-x64-msvc.node` (2.11.4) contains no `CreateJobObjectW` / `AssignProcessToJobObject` / `SetInformationJobObject` / `IsProcessInJob` import strings, so nothing structural holds the tree; it does contain `SetConsoleCtrlHandler`, `CreateProcessW`, `TerminateProcess` and the `Kill-Tree` script.
- Why the stdin pipe (`command.stdin(Stdio::piped())`) does not save it: the pipe does hit EOF when the CLI dies, but Node only emits `'end'` on a stream that is being read, and Vite reads stdin only for its TTY keyboard shortcuts. Minimal check on node 26.7.0: a child with just `process.stdin.on('end', …)` never sees the event after the parent closes the pipe (3 s timeout hit); the same child with `process.stdin.resume()` exits immediately.

Not a duplicate of #10023 (Windows, but there the CLI *exits normally* after a failed compile with `--no-watch`; `on_app_exit` handles `no_watch` today), #1626 (2021, macOS `sh -c`) or #10343 (macOS/Linux Ctrl-C). Because every Node parent has the libuv job behaviour, the wrapper case also hits `concurrently`, nodemon, custom `node scripts/dev.mjs` launchers and IDE task runners, not just a manual `taskkill /F`.

The only code that tears that tree down is `kill_before_dev_process()` (the PowerShell `Kill-Tree`), and it is reachable only from the `ctrlc` console handler and from the CLI's own normal exit paths (`on_app_exit`, the error return of `dev::command`).

So whenever the CLI process ends any other way — `taskkill /F /PID <cli>` without `/T`, `Stop-Process`, Task Manager "End task", `process.kill(pid)` from a Node wrapper, or simply being the direct child of a Node process that exits (libuv puts direct children in a kill-on-close job and terminates them silently) — the whole `cmd /S /C "npm run dev"` → `npm` → `cmd /d /s /c vite` → `node vite.js` → `esbuild` tree survives with a dead parent. Vite keeps `[::1]:1420` and the next `tauri dev` fails with `Port 1420 is already in use`. The frontend never notices the CLI is gone: there is no SIGTERM on Windows, and Vite's `process.stdin.on('end', …)` guard never fires because a non-TTY stdin is never read (`'end'` only fires on a stream that is being consumed).

### Reproduction

Any Vite project — `create-tauri-app` defaults (`beforeDevCommand: "npm run dev"`, `devUrl: "http://localhost:1420"`) are enough.

1. In a terminal: `node node_modules\@tauri-apps\cli\tauri.js dev` (or `npm run tauri dev`; the process to look at is the `node.exe … tauri.js dev` one, which is the CLI).
2. Wait for `VITE … ready`. `netstat -ano | findstr :1420` shows `LISTENING <vite pid>`.
3. Terminate **only** the CLI process: `taskkill /F /PID <pid of node tauri.js>` (no `/T`), or `Stop-Process -Id <pid> -Force`.
4. `netstat -ano | findstr :1420` → still `LISTENING`, same PID. `tasklist` / `Get-CimInstance Win32_Process` still show `cmd /S /C "npm run dev"` → `npm-cli.js run dev` → `cmd /d /s /c vite` → `node vite.js`, with the parent PID pointing at the dead CLI. Run `tauri dev` again → `Port 1420 is already in use`.

Same outcome when the CLI is the direct child of a Node script (`spawn(process.execPath, ['node_modules/@tauri-apps/cli/tauri.js', 'dev'])`) and that script is terminated: libuv's per-process job kills the CLI at once (exit code 0, nothing logged), and everything the CLI spawned through `std::process` is outside that job (`JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_SILENT_BREAKAWAY_OK`) and stays.

Captured on Windows Server 2022 10.0.20348, node 26.7.0, `@tauri-apps/cli` 2.11.4, vite 7.3.6 (timestamps from a script that polls `Get-Process` / `Get-NetTCPConnection` every second; the CLI was launched from `cmd /d /s /c` in its own console, no Node wrapper):

The `beforeDevCommand` tree should end with the CLI regardless of *how* the CLI ends — the way `cargo` already couples its children to itself on Windows. ### Describe the bug

When opening the generated Tauri iOS project in Xcode and running the `app_iOS` target directly, the generated **Build Rust Code** script cannot find `npm` when Node.js is installed through NVM.

The same project works correctly when launched through the Tauri CLI:

```bash
npm run tauri ios dev
```

The issue appears to be caused by the environment/PATH available to Xcode build phases being different from the user's shell environment.

## Environment

* macOS: Apple Silicon
* Node.js: `20.19.0`
* Node manager: NVM
* Project contains `.nvmrc`:

```text
20.19.0
```

* Rust host:

```text
aarch64-apple-darwin
```

* Tauri: 2.x
* Frontend: React + Vite
* Xcode: 26.x
* iOS SDK: 26.x

## Reproduction

1. Create or use a Tauri 2 project with an iOS target.
2. Use NVM to manage Node.js.
3. Add a `.nvmrc` file to the project:

```text
20.19.0
```

4. Verify that the project works from the terminal:

```bash
nvm use
node -v
npm -v
npm run tauri ios dev
```

5. Open the generated Xcode project:

```text
src-tauri/gen/apple/app.xcodeproj
```

6. Select the `app_iOS` target.
7. Run the project directly from Xcode.

The generated Build Phase contains a command similar to:

```bash
npm run -- tauri ios xcode-script -v \
  --platform ${PLATFORM_DISPLAY_NAME:?} \
  --sdk-root ${SDKROOT:?} \
  --framework-search-paths "${FRAMEWORK_SEARCH_PATHS:?}" \
  --header-search-paths "${HEADER_SEARCH_PATHS:?}" \
  --gcc-preprocessor-definitions "${GCC_PREPROCESSOR_DEFINITIONS:-}" \
  --configuration ${CONFIGURATION:?} \
  ${FORCE_COLOR} \
  ${ARCHS:?}
```

## Actual behavior

Xcode fails with:

```text
npm: command not found
```

When `npm` is replaced with the absolute path from NVM:

```text
/Users/<user>/.nvm/versions/node/v20.19.0/bin/npm
```

the next error is:

```text
env: node: No such file or directory
```

Adding the Node installation directory to PATH allows the script to find both Node and npm:

```bash
export PATH="/Users/<user>/.nvm/versions/node/v20.19.0/bin:$PATH"
```

This confirms that the main issue is the environment/PATH available to the Xcode build phase.

## Expected behavior

The generated Tauri Xcode project should be able to locate the Node.js/npm environment required by the project when building from Xcode.

Ideally, when a project uses:

```text
.nvmrc
```

the generated Xcode build script should be able to use the corresponding Node version, or Tauri should provide a documented and reliable mechanism for configuring the Node/npm executable used by Xcode.

## Additional context

The project works correctly when started with:

```bash
npm run tauri ios dev
```

The problem occurs specifically when the generated project is opened directly in Xcode and the build is initiated there.

A related Tauri issue reports a similar problem with `cargo: command not found` in the generated Xcode build phase, where replacing the command with an absolute path works around the PATH problem:

https://github.com/tauri-apps/tauri/issues/10672

## Suggested improvement

Consider making the generated Xcode build phase independent of the user's interactive shell PATH, for example by:

* exposing a configurable Node/npm path;
* resolving the Node version from `.nvmrc`;
* generating an environment script for Xcode;
* or using an absolute project-resolved executable path.

## Logs

Initial error:

```text
/Users/<user>/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/.../Script-XXXXXXXX.sh: line 2: npm: command not found
```

After using the absolute npm path:

```text
env: node: No such file or directory
```

After adding the NVM Node directory to PATH, the Node/npm problem is resolved and the Tauri Xcode script proceeds further.

## Expected outcome

A Tauri iOS project using NVM should be buildable directly from Xcode without manually modifying the generated Build Phase or relying on global PATH configuration.

When opening the generated Tauri iOS project in Xcode and running the `app_iOS` target directly, the generated **Build Rust Code** script cannot find `npm` when Node.js is installed through NVM.

The same project works correctly when launched through the Tauri CLI:

```bash
npm run tauri ios dev
```

The issue appears to be caused by the environment/PATH available to Xcode build phases being different from the user's shell environment.

## Environment

* macOS: Apple Silicon
* Node.js: `20.19.0`
* Node manager: NVM
* Project contains `.nvmrc`:

```text
20.19.0
```

* Rust host:

```text
aarch64-apple-darwin
```

* Tauri: 2.x
* Frontend: React + Vite
* Xcode: 26.x
* iOS SDK: 26.x

## Reproduction

1. Create or use a Tauri 2 project with an iOS target.
2. Use NVM to manage Node.js.
3. Add a `.nvmrc` file to the project:

```text
20.19.0
```

4. Verify that the project works from the terminal:

```bash
nvm use
node -v
npm -v
npm run tauri ios dev
```

5. Open the generated Xcode project:

```text
src-tauri/gen/apple/app.xcodeproj
```

6. Select the `app_iOS` target.
7. Run the project directly from Xcode.

The generated Build Phase contains a command similar to:

```bash
npm run -- tauri ios xcode-script -v \
  --platform ${PLATFORM_DISPLAY_NAME:?} \
  --sdk-root ${SDKROOT:?} \
  --framework-search-paths "${FRAMEWORK_SEARCH_PATHS:?}" \
  --header-search-paths "${HEADER_SEARCH_PATHS:?}" \
  --gcc-preprocessor-definitions "${GCC_PREPROCESSOR_DEFINITIONS:-}" \
  --configuration ${CONFIGURATION:?} \
  ${FORCE_COLOR} \
  ${ARCHS:?}
```

## Actual behavior

Xcode fails with:

```text
npm: command not found
```

When `npm` is replaced with the absolute path from NVM:

```text
/Users/<user>/.nvm/versions/node/v20.19.0/bin/npm
```

the next error is:

```text
env: node: No such file or directory
```

Adding the Node installation directory to PATH allows the script to find both Node and npm:

```bash
export PATH="/Users/<user>/.nvm/versions/node/v20.19.0/bin:$PATH"
```

This confirms that the main issue is the environment/PATH available to the Xcode build phase.

## Expected behavior

The generated Tauri Xcode project should be able to locate the Node.js/npm environment required by the project when building from Xcode.

Ideally, when a project uses:

```text
.nvmrc
```

the generated Xcode build script should be able to use the corresponding Node version, or Tauri should provide a documented and reliable mechanism for configuring the Node/npm executable used by Xcode.

## Additional context

The project works correctly when started with:

```bash
npm run tauri ios dev
```

The problem occurs specifically when the generated project is opened directly in Xcode and the build is initiated there.

A related Tauri issue reports a similar problem with `cargo: command not found` in the generated Xcode build phase, where replacing the command with an absolute path works around the PATH problem:

https://github.com/tauri-apps/tauri/issues/10672

## Suggested improvement

Consider making the generated Xcode build phase independent of the user's interactive shell PATH, for example by:

* exposing a configurable Node/npm path;
* resolving the Node version from `.nvmrc`;
* generating an environment script for Xcode;
* or using an absolute project-resolved executable path.

```

After using the absolute npm path:

```text
env: node: No such file or directory
```

After adding the NVM Node directory to PATH, the Node/npm problem is resolved and the Tauri Xcode script proceeds further.

## Expected outcome

A Tauri iOS project using NVM should be buildable directly from Xcode without manually modifying the generated Build Phase or relying on global PATH configuration.

### Describe the problem

When running Tauri mobile development commands and multiple physical devices or simulators are available, Tauri may automatically select one device instead of interactively asking the developer which device should be used.

This can be inconvenient when both a physical device and a simulator are available.

## Example: iOS

My development machine had both a physical iPhone and an iOS Simulator available:

```text
== Devices ==

MacBook Pro de Luis
iPhone de Luis (17.7.1)

== Simulators ==

iPhone 15 (26.3.1)
```

The iPhone simulator had the identifier:

```text
76BDA1C1-2D8E-415A-A57B-939EE4C71599
```

The physical iPhone was also available to Xcode, including wireless connectivity.

Running:

```bash
npm run tauri ios dev
```

could select the physical device automatically.

To use the simulator, I had to explicitly provide the device:

```bash
npm run tauri ios dev -- "76BDA1C1-2D8E-415A-A57B-939EE4C71599"
```

## Expected behavior

When multiple compatible destinations are available, Tauri could optionally display an interactive selection:

```text
Multiple devices found:

1. iPhone de Luis (iOS 17.7.1) [physical]
2. iPhone 15 (iOS 26.3.1) [simulator]

Select device:
>
```

The selected destination would then be used for the development session.

## Why this is useful

Physical iOS devices can remain available to Xcode over Wi-Fi even after the USB cable has been disconnected.

For example:

```text
Physical iPhone: connected
iOS Simulator: booted
```

In this situation, automatic selection may not match the developer's intention.

The same situation can occur with multiple Android devices/emulators.

## Desired behavior

When more than one valid device is detected:

1. Detect all available devices.
2. Show their platform, type and name.
3. Allow the developer to select one interactively.
4. Continue normally after selection.

A non-interactive option should still be available for scripts/CI, for example:

```bash
tauri ios dev "<UDID>"
```

which already provides an explicit way to select a destination.

## Cross-platform scope

This would be useful for both:

```text
iOS
- physical devices
- simulators

Android
- physical devices
- emulators
```

## Related discussion

There is already a Tauri discussion proposing simulator/device pre-selection via the command line, including the problem of working with multiple simulators:

https://github.com/tauri-apps/tauri/discussions/9664

## Expected outcome

Tauri should provide a convenient interactive destination-selection experience when multiple mobile devices are available, while preserving explicit device selection for automation and CI.


### Describe the solution you'd like

My development machine had both a physical iPhone and an iOS Simulator available:

Multiple devices found:

1. iPhone de Luis (iOS 17.7.1) [physical]
2. iPhone 15 (iOS 26.3.1) [simulator]

Select device:
>

On Linux the webview is WebKitGTK, whose inspector speaks its own protocol rather than CDP. Nothing automatable can attach: no Playwright, no puppeteer, no chrome-devtools MCP server. Automated UI verification of a Tauri app on Linux is effectively impossible.

## Suggestion

Anything that lets an external process drive and observe the webview over a documented protocol:

- a CDP shim over the WebKit inspector protocol, even a partial one (DOM query, evaluate, screenshot, console),
- or a first-class `tauri::Webview::evaluate_with_result` plus console/event streaming on a socket, which a test harness can drive without CDP at all.

The second is probably cheaper and would cover most of what a smoke test needs.

body_text:
Under Xvfb with software GL, the window opens and renders nothing. No error, no warning, no log line. Setting `WEBKIT_DISABLE_COMPOSITING_MODE=1` fixes it completely.

## Environment

- Linux (Debian 13, x86_64), WebKitGTK 2.52.3, Xvfb 1920x1080x24, fluxbox, no GPU.
- tauri 2.11.1.

## Before and after

Without the variable: a white window, correct title, correct size, DOM present in the inspector, nothing painted. With `WEBKIT_DISABLE_COMPOSITING_MODE=1` (also with `WEBKIT_DISABLE_DMABUF_RENDERER=1` and `LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1`): renders correctly, first try.

It took me a while to figure this out, assuming my own asset pipeline was at fault, because a blank window and a 404'd bundle look identical.

## Suggestion

Tauri knows more about the environment than the app author does. When compositing is unavailable or the GL renderer is software, either set the variable or log one line saying the webview was created without compositing and naming the escape hatch.

## Related

#9304, #8655, #10011 and #12361 report the blank-window symptom itself (NVIDIA/DMABUF, Wayland); this issue is about the missing diagnostic, which none of them covers.

A request for a path that is not in `frontendDist` returns **HTTP 200 with `Content-Type: text/html`** (the SPA fallback serving `index.html`). For a module request that turns "file not found" into `'text/html' is not a valid JavaScript MIME type`, and the offending URL appears nowhere in the error.

A missing module is a common way a desktop app fails to boot. Today that failure names neither the file nor the reason.

## Environment

tauri 2.11.1, tauri-build 2.6, Linux (Debian 13, x86_64), WebKitGTK 2.52.3, GTK 3.24.49.
`WebviewUrl::App("/index.html")` over a static `frontendDist` of ES modules with an inline import map.

## Scope

This applies whenever the `tauri://` protocol serves `frontendDist:` production builds, and dev without devUrl. With devUrl set, the webview talks to the dev server directly and this code path is not involved. The CLI's built-in dev server (static frontendDist in dev) implements the same fallback chain and fails identically.

## Evidence

Probed from inside the webview:

```
probe main.js                 -> 200 text/javascript  @ tauri://localhost/main.js
probe preload.js              -> 200 text/javascript  @ tauri://localhost/preload.js
probe definitely-not-here.js  -> 200 text/html        @ tauri://localhost/definitely-not-here.js
```

The last line is the problem. A path that exists nowhere returns `200 text/html`.

The symptom was a window rendering its splash screen forever, with one diagnostic:

```
[boot] import failed, retrying once cache-busted: 'text/html' is not a valid JavaScript MIME type.
```

Nothing further was reported. The retry (same specifier plus a `?cache-bust` query) neither resolved nor rejected while watching, so the boot promise never settled. I didn't establish whether the query string is handled differently.

I've ended up injecting an init script that fetches every import-map target and reports which ones come back as HTML.

## Why it matters

`200 text/html` is indistinguishable from success at the protocol level, and the resulting MIME error names no URL, so the failure is invisible to the tooling that would otherwise catch it. A 404 is machine readable and can be easily caught by CI.

## Suggestion

Do not fall back for requests that are clearly not navigations. `Sec-Fetch-Dest: script`, the `Accept` header, or a `.js`/`.mjs`/`.css`/`.json` extension is enough to answer 404 instead of serving `index.html`. SPA fallback is right for a navigation and harmful for a subresource.

Failing that, warn from the protocol handler when it falls back, naming the requested path.

No config or builder option disables the fallback today. The closest workaround is rewriting the response in on_web_resource_request when a subresource path comes back as `text/html`, which is the heuristic this issue argues the framework should apply itself.

A command listed in `invoke_handler!` but missing from `COMMANDS` in the plugin's build script is silently unreachable. No permission file is generated for it, so no capability can grant it, so every invoke is rejected at runtime. No warnings at build time.

## Background

My plugin had this:

```rust
// build.rs
const COMMANDS: &[&str] = &["do_something"];   // debug_log missing

// lib.rs
.invoke_handler(tauri::generate_handler![commands::do_something, commands::debug_log])
```

`debug_log` was documented in our own contributor docs as the way to forward frontend logs to the backend.
It had never worked, because of that one missing string. Every invoke was rejected, our JS caught the rejection, and the channel looked simply quiet.

Two steps were needed, and the second is easy to miss even once you know:

1. add the name to `COMMANDS` so the permission is generated
2. then grant `allow-debug-log` in `permissions/default.toml`

Generating the permission file does not grant it.

## Suggestion

`generate_handler!` knows the command names, the build script knows `COMMANDS`.
A build-time warning when a handler-registered command has no generated permission would have saved the whole detour.

An error would be defensible too, since the command is unreachable either way.

Secondary: a runtime log line when an invoke is rejected for a missing permission, rather than only an `Err` the caller may swallow.

### Describe the bug

We ship a desktop-pet style game (transparent always-on-top window is its core form factor): a large (1440×900) `transparent: true`, `alwaysOnTop: true`, `decorations: false`, `shadow: false` window rendering a WebGL (PixiJS) scene on a transparent canvas (`backgroundAlpha: 0`), with HTML div UI on top. Because it is a desktop pet, we frequently toggle `set_ignore_cursor_events()` as the cursor moves in/out of the interactive region (a "cursor event guard": transparent areas of the window are click-through, the canvas area is interactive).

Players on **Windows 10** report two sporadic rendering failures, both observed in player-recorded videos:

1. **Desktop wallpaper turns black while the app is minimized, and restores when the window is brought back.** The wallpaper file itself is never modified — purely a display failure that self-recovers with the window state change.
2. **The window's transparent areas turn black during normal interaction** (e.g. opening a UI panel, entering item-placement mode, moving the cursor across the canvas boundary) — exactly the moments our app toggles `set_ignore_cursor_events()`.

Both are low-probability events under high-frequency triggers: the vast majority of toggles/minimizes render correctly.

### Expected behavior

Transparent regions and the desktop wallpaper should stay correctly composed on Windows 10 when toggling `set_ignore_cursor_events` or minimizing/restoring a transparent always-on-top window.

### Analysis (from reading tao 0.34.8 sources)

- `tao/src/platform_impl/windows/window.rs` — when `attributes.transparent && !pl_attribs.no_redirection_bitmap`, tao enables the legacy `DwmEnableBlurBehindWindow` + empty-region `(0, 0, -1, -1)` hack for full-window transparency.
- `tao/src/platform_impl/windows/window_state.rs` — `set_ignore_cursor_events` toggles `WS_EX_TRANSPARENT | WS_EX_LAYERED` via `SetWindowLongPtr`, forcing DWM to rebuild the composition tree (layered ⇄ direct composition path).

Our working model: BlurBehind hack + frequent `WS_EX_LAYERED` toggles (cursor guard) + minimize/restore of a large always-on-top transparent window occasionally race with DWM's composition-tree rebuild on Windows 10, losing either the window's alpha or the wallpaper layer (WorkerW) for a moment — the "black" being an invalid/uninitialized surface. We are still correlating occurrences with `dwm.exe` events in the Windows Event Log to determine whether DWM actually restarts or this is a non-crash composition failure, so the model above is our best current hypothesis rather than a confirmed root cause.

### Relation to #15410

`noRedirectionBitmap` (`WS_EX_NOREDIRECTIONBITMAP` / DirectComposition path) looks like the structural fix for this class of issue: it sidesteps the BlurBehind hack entirely. Questions for maintainers:

1. Which release will include #15410 — a 2.12.0? Any chance of a backport to 2.11.x?
2. Are you aware of other Windows 10 reports where toggling `set_ignore_cursor_events` or minimizing transparent windows corrupts composition (black wallpaper / black transparent areas)? Possibly related: #12849, #11284.

### Platform and Versions

- tauri: 2.10.3 (tao 0.34.8, wry 0.48.0)
- OS: Windows 10 (player reports so far; exact builds + GPU/driver info being collected)
- WebView2 runtime: affected machines' versions being collected
- Frontend: PixiJS 8 WebGL canvas (`backgroundAlpha: 0`, `preference: 'webgl'`), HTML div UI coexisting in the same transparent window

### Additional context

- App: "PicoCat", a Steam desktop-pet / idle game.
- We plan mitigations on our side (hide-to-tray instead of minimize; debouncing cursor-event toggles), but the underlying composition path seems worth flagging upstream.
- Happy to provide player videos / Windows Event Log data once collected.

body_text:
### Describe the problem

If you use the uninstaller in silent mode (parameter `/S`), there is no option to enable the deletion of the application data.

### Describe the solution you'd like

~~Add an option to tauri.conf.json that allows this behaviour to be controlled.~~
I suggest adding an uninstaller CLI flag /DELETEAPPDATA.

**Why a CLI flag instead of a config option:**
- Whether app data should be removed is usually decided by whoever runs the uninstaller (e.g. a package manager like Chocolatey, or an IT deployment script), not at build time.
- It matches how the other uninstaller options (/P, /UPDATE) already work.
- The change is small and self-contained in installer.nsi.

**Proposed behaviour:**
- uninstall.exe /S /DELETEAPPDATA (or /P /DELETEAPPDATA) deletes the app data, just like checking "Delete the application data" in the UI.
- In interactive mode, /DELETEAPPDATA pre-checks that checkbox. The user can still uncheck it.
- It has no effect together with /UPDATE, which keeps the current behaviour of never deleting app data during updates.

### Alternatives considered

The behaviour can already be achieved today with the NSIS installer hooks (bundle > windows > nsis > installerHooks), since NSIS_HOOK_PREUNINSTALL runs before the app data check:

```
!macro NSIS_HOOK_PREUNINSTALL
  ${GetOptions} $CMDLINE "/DELETEAPPDATA" $R0
  ${IfNot} ${Errors}
    StrCpy $DeleteAppDataCheckboxState 1
  ${EndIf}
!macroend
```


Caveat: This relies on the internal Tauri variable $DeleteAppDataCheckboxState and may break with any Tauri update

### Additional context

### Describe the bug


Calling requestFullscreen() puts the document into fullscreen within the webview, but does not fullscreen the containing native Tauri window. The native window remains decorated and keeps its original size and position.

This seems to be unimplimented as CEF `DisplayHandler` does not implement `on_fullscreen_mode_change`



### Reproduction

```document.documentElement.requestFullscreen();```

### Expected behavior

Native window enters borderless fullscreen.

body_text:
### Describe the bug

On Android, events emitted by a custom plugin never reach their JavaScript listeners.
Registration succeeds, the native side fires and delivers the event, but the JS callback
registered with `addPluginListener` is never invoked. No error is thrown.

This is a regression correlated with the `tauri-codegen` / `tauri-macros` version pair:

| `tauri-codegen` / `tauri-macros` | Result                     |
| -------------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| 2.5.5 / 2.5.5                    | ✅ JS listeners fire       |
| 2.6.3 / 2.6.3                    | ❌ JS listeners never fire |

The `tauri` crate stayed at 2.10.1 (and 2.10.3) throughout. The JS code, the plugin
revision, and the generated Android project were unchanged between the two runs.


### Reproduction

1. Android Tauri v2 app, `tauri` pinned 2.10.1, `tauri-build` 2.5.6.

2. Custom Android plugin (`music-notification`) that emits events from a native
   `BroadcastReceiver` when the Android media session's Next action is dispatched.

3. In JS, register listeners on mount:

   ```js
   await Promise.all([
     onPlay(...), onPause(...), onNext(...), onPrev(...),
     onPreviousAlbumNeeded(...), onQueueEnded(...),
   ]);
   // implemented as: core.addPluginListener("music-notification", "onNext", cb)
   ```

4. Press Play, then trigger Next from the media notification (or call the plugin's
   `next()` command directly — both reproduce).

5. Switch the dependency pair and repeat:

   ```
   cargo update -p tauri-codegen --precise 2.5.5
   cargo update -p tauri-macros  --precise 2.5.5   # listeners fire (fixed)
   cargo update -p tauri-codegen --precise 2.6.3
   cargo update -p tauri-macros  --precise 2.6.3   # listeners dead (broken)
   ```

   Note: with `tauri = "=2.10.1"`, a fresh resolve picks 2.6.3 for this pair
   automatically — no `tauri` upgrade is needed to trigger the bug.

Plugin source: https://github.com/AverTry/tauri-plugin-music-notification
(revision `21ed5d7b42ea14832e09cdb204bcfbc957313937`, consumed as a local `path`
dependency). The Kotlin service sends a local broadcast; the plugin's
`BroadcastReceiver.onReceive` receives it and triggers the event.


### Expected behavior

With `tauri-codegen`/`tauri-macros` 2.6.3, the JS callback should fire exactly as it
does with 2.5.5. Native event emission is identical in both cases.


### Full `tauri info` output

```text
**Broken (codegen/macros 2.6.3)** — native emits, plugin receives, JS is silent:


D/MusicPlayerService: Sent broadcast: eventName=onNext, action=next, currentIndex=5, isPlaying=false, trackId=5
D/MusicNotificationPlugin: BroadcastReceiver.onReceive called with action: MUSIC_NOTIFICATION_EVENT
D/MusicNotificationPlugin: Event received: eventName=onNext, action=next, currentIndex=5, isPlaying=false, trackId=5



[AUDIO] >>> all 6 listeners registered        // ← no "onNext FIRED" ever follows


**Working (codegen/macros 2.5.5)** — identical native side, and the JS callback runs:


D/MusicNotificationPlugin: Event received: eventName=onNext, action=next, currentIndex=5, isPlaying=true, trackId=5



[AUDIO] onNext FIRED [object Object]
[AUDIO] onNext -> handleAudioPageChange(1)


User-visible effect: the reader screen does not advance when Next is pressed.
```

### Stack trace

```text
No exception or Rust panic is produced. There is no ACL/permission error at event
delivery time. The only unusual console output is this, present in both working and
broken runs and believed unrelated to the regression:


Uncaught (in promise) notification.is_permission_granted not allowed on window "main",
webview "main", URL: about:blank
referenced by: capability: default / mobile-capability, permission: allow-is-permission-granted
```

### Additional context


**Exact dependency set (identical in both runs unless stated):**

```toml
tauri = { version = "=2.10.1", features = ["protocol-asset"] }
tauri-build = { version = "=2.5.6", features = [] }
tauri-runtime = "=2.10.1"
tauri-runtime-wry = "=2.10.1"
```

Resolved, and identical in both the working and broken runs:

```
tauri              2.10.1
tauri-build         2.5.6
tauri-runtime       2.10.1
tauri-runtime-wry   2.10.1
tauri-utils         2.9.3
tauri-plugin        2.5.4
@tauri-apps/api     ⟨version⟩
@tauri-apps/cli     ⟨version⟩
```

The only variables between working and broken are `tauri-codegen` and `tauri-macros`
(2.5.5 → 2.6.3).

**Other things already ruled out by testing:**

- `tauri` crate: 2.10.1 and 2.10.3 both reproduce. `tauri` 2.11.x reproduces.
- `tauri-utils`: 2.8.3 and 2.9.3 both fine.
- `tauri-plugin`: stayed at 2.5.4 the whole time.
- JavaScript side: untouched between runs.

{"repository": "tauri-apps/tauri", "task_candidate_id": 24735, "repository_id": 292, "issue_number": 16031, "github_issue_id": 5466438254, "html_url": "https://github.com/tauri-apps/tauri/issues/16031", "created_at": "2026-09-15T19:22:26+00:00", "author_association": "NONE", "title": "[bug] Android: custom plugin events never reach `addPluginListener` JS callbacks when tauri-codegen + tauri-macros are 2.6.x (works with 2.5.5)", "body_text": "### Describe the bug

On Android, events emitted by a custom plugin never reach their JavaScript listeners.
Registration succeeds, the native side fires and delivers the event, but the JS callback
registered with `addPluginListener` is never invoked. No error is thrown.

This is a regression correlated with the `tauri-codegen` / `tauri-macros` version pair:

| `tauri-codegen` / `tauri-macros` | Result                     |
| -------------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| 2.5.5 / 2.5.5                    | ✅ JS listeners fire       |
| 2.6.3 / 2.6.3                    | ❌ JS listeners never fire |

The `tauri` crate stayed at 2.10.1 (and 2.10.3) throughout. The JS code, the plugin
revision, and the generated Android project were unchanged between the two runs.


### Reproduction

1. Android Tauri v2 app, `tauri` pinned 2.10.1, `tauri-build` 2.5.6.

2. Custom Android plugin (`music-notification`) that emits events from a native
   `BroadcastReceiver` when the Android media session's Next action is dispatched.

3. In JS, register listeners on mount:

   ```js
   await Promise.all([
     onPlay(...), onPause(...), onNext(...), onPrev(...),
     onPreviousAlbumNeeded(...), onQueueEnded(...),
   ]);
   // implemented as: core.addPluginListener("music-notification", "onNext", cb)
   ```

4. Press Play, then trigger Next from the media notification (or call the plugin's
   `next()` command directly — both reproduce).

5. Switch the dependency pair and repeat:

   ```
   cargo update -p tauri-codegen --precise 2.5.5
   cargo update -p tauri-macros  --precise 2.5.5   # listeners fire (fixed)
   cargo update -p tauri-codegen --precise 2.6.3
   cargo update -p tauri-macros  --precise 2.6.3   # listeners dead (broken)
   ```

   Note: with `tauri = "=2.10.1"`, a fresh resolve picks 2.6.3 for this pair
   automatically — no `tauri` upgrade is needed to trigger the bug.

Plugin source: https://github.com/AverTry/tauri-plugin-music-notification
(revision `21ed5d7b42ea14832e09cdb204bcfbc957313937`, consumed as a local `path`
dependency). The Kotlin service sends a local broadcast; the plugin's
`BroadcastReceiver.onReceive` receives it and triggers the event.


### Expected behavior

With `tauri-codegen`/`tauri-macros` 2.6.3, the JS callback should fire exactly as it
does with 2.5.5. Native event emission is identical in both cases.


### Full `tauri info` output

```text
**Broken (codegen/macros 2.6.3)** — native emits, plugin receives, JS is silent:


D/MusicPlayerService: Sent broadcast: eventName=onNext, action=next, currentIndex=5, isPlaying=false, trackId=5
D/MusicNotificationPlugin: BroadcastReceiver.onReceive called with action: MUSIC_NOTIFICATION_EVENT
D/MusicNotificationPlugin: Event received: eventName=onNext, action=next, currentIndex=5, isPlaying=false, trackId=5



[AUDIO] >>> all 6 listeners registered        // ← no "onNext FIRED" ever follows


**Working (codegen/macros 2.5.5)** — identical native side, and the JS callback runs:


D/MusicNotificationPlugin: Event received: eventName=onNext, action=next, currentIndex=5, isPlaying=true, trackId=5



[AUDIO] onNext FIRED [object Object]
[AUDIO] onNext -> handleAudioPageChange(1)


User-visible effect: the reader screen does not advance when Next is pressed.
```

### Stack trace

```text
No exception or Rust panic is produced. There is no ACL/permission error at event
delivery time. The only unusual console output is this, present in both working and
broken runs and believed unrelated to the regression:


Uncaught (in promise) notification.is_permission_granted not allowed on window "main",
webview "main", URL: about:blank
referenced by: capability: default / mobile-capability, permission: allow-is-permission-granted
```

**Exact dependency set (identical in both runs unless stated):**

```toml
tauri = { version = "=2.10.1", features = ["protocol-asset"] }
tauri-build = { version = "=2.5.6", features = [] }
tauri-runtime = "=2.10.1"

```

Resolved, and identical in both the working and broken runs:

```

tauri-utils         2.9.3

@tauri-apps/api     ⟨version⟩

```

The only variables between working and broken are `tauri-codegen` and `tauri-macros`
(2.5.5 → 2.6.3).

- JavaScript side: untouched between runs.
- `tauri-runtime` / `tauri-runtime-wry`: forced to 2.10.1 via direct exact
  dependencies, which does **not** fix it.
- Not a lockdown/ACL error — registration is not rejected, the event is simply

### Describe the problem

This is specific to `svelte` & `sveltekit` and might not benefit anyone else outside of those using this framework.

When sending an `ipc` request as part of a `sveltekit` [`load`](https://svelte.dev/docs/kit/load#Making-fetch-requests) function `svelte` will complain that:

```
Loading ipc://localhost/TauRPC__Provider.get_providers using `window.fetch`. For best results, use the `fetch` that is passed to your `load` function: https://svelte.dev/docs/kit/load#making-fetch-requests
```

This is because the `sendIpcMessage()` uses the native `fetch()` of the webview in use.

```ts
function sendIpcMessage(message) {
    const { cmd, callback, error, payload, options } = message

    if (
      !customProtocolIpcFailed
      && (canUseCustomProtocol || cmd === fetchChannelDataCommand)
    ) {
      const { contentType, data } = processIpcMessage(payload)

      const headers = new Headers((options && options.headers) || {})
      headers.set('Content-Type', contentType)
      headers.set('Tauri-Callback', callback)
      headers.set('Tauri-Error', error)
      headers.set('Tauri-Invoke-Key', __TAURI_INVOKE_KEY__)

      fetch(window.__TAURI_INTERNALS__.convertFileSrc(cmd, 'ipc'), {
        method: 'POST',
        body: data,
        headers
      })
```

`Svelte` however, would like you to use their supplied `fetch` as it offers the following & even warns that things might be inconsistent or otherwise affected when not used:

```
fetch: {
    (input: RequestInfo | URL, init?: RequestInit): Promise<Response>;
    (input: string | URL | Request, init?: RequestInit): Promise<Response>;
}

fetch is equivalent to the [native fetch web API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/fetch), with a few additional features:

    It can be used to make credentialed requests on the server, as it inherits the cookie and authorization headers for the page request.
    It can make relative requests on the server (ordinarily, fetch requires a URL with an origin when used in a server context).
    Internal requests (e.g. for +server.js routes) go directly to the handler function when running on the server, without the overhead of an HTTP call.
    During server-side rendering, the response will be captured and inlined into the rendered HTML by hooking into the text and json methods of the Response object. Note that headers will not be serialized, unless explicitly included via [filterSerializedResponseHeaders](https://svelte.dev/docs/kit/hooks#handle)
    During hydration, the response will be read from the HTML, guaranteeing consistency and preventing an additional network request.

You can learn more about making credentialed requests with cookies [here](https://svelte.dev/docs/kit/load#Cookies)
``` 

### Describe the solution you'd like

I'm not too familiar with the internals of `tauri`, but maybe it is possible to allow `invoke` to accept a custom `fetch` implementation for specific cases like these.

The already exists an `InvokeOptions` interface for `invoke` calls to add custom headers if necessary. This could perhaps be extended to also accept an implementation of `fetch`

### Alternatives considered

The only alternatives to suppress these `warnings` are to 
- not use `sveltekits` [`load`](https://svelte.dev/docs/kit/load) functions for any request made using `tauri's` `ipc` mechanism & integrate them as regular calls within the components which required them
or
- simply ignore them outright

Since `load` functions are an integral part of the framework & affect / interact with a wide range of features provided by `sveltekit` they would be hard to give up for any user of the framework. 

And ignoring them becomes quite hard as any "page" that requires `ipc` calls triggers these warnings for each individual request made.

### Additional context

Changes required would be something like this:

[ipc-protocol.js](https://github.com/tauri-apps/tauri/blob/f45ec0dcf83c139c8fdde5e61923a0e82836f756/crates/tauri/scripts/ipc-protocol.js#L37)
```ts
let trueFetch = fetch
if (options.fetchImpl !== undefined) trueFetch = options.fetchImpl

trueFetch(window.__TAURI_INTERNALS__.convertFileSrc(cmd, 'ipc'), {
``` 

[core.ts](https://github.com/tauri-apps/tauri/blob/f45ec0dcf83c139c8fdde5e61923a0e82836f756/packages/api/src/core.ts#L232)
```ts
/**
 * @since 2.0.0
 */
interface InvokeOptions {
  headers: HeadersInit
  fetchImpl?: (input: RequestInfo | URL, init?: RequestInit) => Promise<Response>
}
```

body_text:
### Describe the problem

I'm building a Tauri app for Windows and finding the current NSIS bundler a bit painful to work with when I need anything beyond the basics. NSIS scripts are hard to read and maintain, and customizing install behavior (custom pages, conditional logic, upgrade flows) quickly turns into a mess. I know I can post-process with a custom `.iss` and `iscc`, but that means losing all the native integration Tauri already has—auto-injected paths, WebView2 handling, versioning, updater markers.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Add Inno Setup as a first-class Windows bundle target (e.g. `tauri build --bundles inno`), alongside the existing NSIS and WiX options.

Inno Setup has a few things going for it that make it worth considering:

- Pascal Script is way more readable and maintainable than NSIS's stack-based syntax
- Built-in `AppId` + version upgrade handling (no manual registry gymnastics)
- Excellent silent install support out of the box (`/VERYSILENT`, `/SILENT`)
- Mature code-signing and multi-language UI
- Used by large desktop apps (VS Code, Discord, etc.) so it's well-tested in the wild

The implementation would follow the same pattern as the NSIS backend—configurable `.iss` template, variable injection from `tauri.conf.json`, invoke `iscc` during bundle, handle WebView2 bootstrapper, proper uninstall/upgrade registration.

This wouldn't replace NSIS, just give people another option.

### Alternatives considered

1. **Post-build script calling `iscc` manually** — works for a basic install/uninstall, but I lose WebView2 integration, updater bundle markers, and have to manually keep paths/versions in sync with `tauri.conf.json`. It's fragile.
2. **Stick with NSIS** — it works, but the scripting experience is rough and customizing behavior gets ugly fast.
3. **WiX/MSI** — doesn't fit my use case; I want a single exe installer, not an MSI, and WiX has its own complexity.

### Additional context

### Describe the problem

Google has just announced Googlebook, a new desktop platform:

https://googlebook.google/

For developers maintaining cross-platform Tauri applications, there is currently no clear guidance on how Googlebook should be targeted.

Since Tauri already supports both desktop Linux and Android, it would be useful to clarify whether Googlebook is expected to work through one of these existing targets, or whether first-class Googlebook support would require additional platform-specific integration.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Consider supporting Googlebook as an officially supported Tauri target platform, if technically feasible.

At this early stage, guidance from the Tauri team would also be helpful on the expected path for Googlebook support — for example, whether applications should target Googlebook through the existing Android or Linux support, or whether a dedicated Googlebook target and platform-specific integration may be necessary.

### Alternatives considered

One possible alternative is using Tauri's existing Android target and distributing the application as an Android application on Googlebook, assuming Googlebook provides sufficient compatibility and desktop integration.

Another possibility is using the existing Linux desktop build through Googlebook's Linux environment.

However, either approach may differ from first-class platform support in areas such as window management, filesystem access, menus, keyboard shortcuts, application lifecycle, and other desktop integrations.

### Additional context

Googlebook was announced only about 1 hour ago at the time of filing this issue, so I understand that it is extremely early and that the exact scope or feasibility of Tauri support may not yet be known.

Official Googlebook website:

https://googlebook.google/

This issue is primarily intended to start a discussion about compatibility and how the Tauri project intends to approach this new platform.

body_text:
### Describe the bug

`tauri android build` on a Windows host aborts before Gradle ever runs, because
`cargo-mobile2` (which `tauri-cli` pins at `0.22.5`) creates the `jniLibs`
symlinks unconditionally. Creating a symlink on Windows requires
`SeCreateSymbolicLinkPrivilege` or Developer Mode, so on a stock Windows
machine — and on many corporate machines where Developer Mode is disabled by
policy — the whole build fails with no fallback and no flag to opt out:

```text
Error failed to build Android app: Failed to create a symbolic link from
"target\debug\...\lib<app>lib.so" to "app\src\main\jniLibs\x86_64\lib<app>lib.so"
(file clobbering enabled): Creation symbolic link is not allowed for this system.
```

The call sites are `cargo-mobile2`'s `src/android/jnilibs.rs` (`force_symlink`
for the built `.so`) and `src/android/project.rs` (`force_symlink_relative` for
the asset dir); both funnel into `src/os/windows/ln.rs`.

The symlinked file is consumed immediately afterwards by the Gradle packaging
step, so a plain copy is semantically identical for this use — the build does
not need the link to be a real link.

A fix is already open: https://github.com/tauri-apps/cargo-mobile2/pull/527
(fall back to `std::fs::copy` when symlink creation fails with
`ERROR_PRIVILEGE_NOT_HELD`, plus a `log::warn!` so users know why they did not
get a real symlink). It has sat since 2026-09-13 with both CI runs stuck at
`action_required`, i.e. waiting for a maintainer to approve the workflow run for
a first-time contributor — so it may simply have fallen through the cracks
rather than been rejected.

### Reproduction

1. A Windows 10/11 host **without** Developer Mode and without
   `SeCreateSymbolicLinkPrivilege`. (Developer Mode is off by default; you can
   confirm the missing privilege by running `mklink "a.txt" "b.txt"` in a plain
   `cmd` window as a normal user — it reports *A required privilege is not held
   by the client.*)
2. In any Tauri 2 project: `pnpm tauri android init`
3. `pnpm tauri android build --debug --apk --target x86_64`

Expected: the APK builds. Actual: it fails with the error above, before any
Rust/Gradle compilation of the app itself. Enabling Developer Mode or running
elevated makes it pass, which is what points at the symlink call.


### Expected behavior

When the privilege is missing, materialize the artifact in `jniLibs` by copying
and warn, instead of failing the build. Hosts that do have the privilege keep
getting real symlinks, so nothing changes for them.

### Stack trace

```text
Error failed to build Android app: Failed to create a symbolic link from ... (file clobbering enabled): Creation symbolic link is not allowed for this system.


Originates in `cargo-mobile2::os::windows::ln::force_symlink`, surfaced through
`tauri-cli`'s Android build path.
```

### Additional context

This is the next blocker in the same chain as
https://github.com/tauri-apps/tauri/pull/16017 — `ensure_gradlew` gated its
CRLF-to-LF rewrite behind `#[cfg(unix)]`, so a `gradlew` checked out with CRLF
broke `sh ./gradlew` on Windows hosts too. That one was merged into `dev` as
`5d995ed` on 2026-09-21. We hit them in that exact order while building an
Android APK from a Windows host: first the CRLF failure, then this symlink
failure once the CLI was patched locally.

Two follow-ups, if convenient:

1. Could someone approve the workflow run on tauri-apps/cargo-mobile2#527 and give
   it a look? It is a small, contained fallback, and it is the difference between
   "Android builds on Windows" and "Android does not build on Windows" for
   anyone without Developer Mode.
2. `tauri-v2.11.5` and `tauri-v2.11.6` both still ship the old `#[cfg(unix)]`-gated
   `ensure_gradlew`, and the newest published `@tauri-apps/cli` is 2.11.5
   (published 2026-09-20, the day *before* the merge). Is there a plan to carry
   #16017 into a 2.x patch release, or is `dev`/v3-only intentional so that 2.x
   users are expected to fix it on their own side?

### Describe the bug

Xcode v27 seems to set a few extra policy requirements, that the current Tauri latest version can't handle.

Also captured here:
https://github.com/tauri-apps/tao/issues/1340
However, I think it deserves an issue on the main repo, as this issue effectively makes it impossible to run tauri projects on ios, with a fresh install.

I'll be honest, I'm not very knowledgeable about iOS, so I can't really contribute to the discussion.

At the same time, right now Tauri is not usable to cleanly build iOS apps following the tutorials.
It also looks to me like there's further moving pieces on the table, maybe other parts needs a patch as well. If someone has in-depth knowledge about iOS part of Tauri, please review compatibility with Xcode 27...

### Reproduction

Install tauri in an empty project, with latest version of Xcode.
First you have to bump the min version for ios, and then it fails with
"The capability “Install Application” is not supported by this device."

### Expected behavior

Bundles & can run the app in simulator.

### Summary

`TrayIconBuilder::on_menu_event` is **global**, not tray-scoped. An app that registers a handler on both the app `Builder` and the tray builder gets that handler invoked **twice for every menu event in the application** — including events from the app menu that have nothing to do with the tray.

The naming and the receiver both imply tray scope, and a correctly tray-scoped vector exists three lines away in the same struct literal, so the incorrect reading is the one a careful reader arrives at.

### Version

`tauri 2.11.3`, macOS. Read from the vendored source in the cargo registry.

### The mechanism

Both registrations land in the **same** `Vec`:

- `src/tray/mod.rs:427-434` — `TrayIcon::register` pushes its `on_menu_event` handler into `app_handle.manager.`**`menu`**`.global_event_listeners`.
- `src/app.rs:2004` — `Builder::on_menu_event` pushes into `menu_event_listeners`, which becomes that same vector via `src/app.rs:2261` → `src/manager/mod.rs:311`.
- `src/app.rs:2588-2596` — on `EventLoopMessage::MenuEvent`, every listener in that vector is invoked, for every menu event.

### Why the wrong reading is the reasonable one

`src/manager/mod.rs:301-313` constructs `TrayManager` and `MenuManager` adjacently, and **both carry a field named `global_event_listeners`** (plus one named `event_listeners`):

```rust
tray: tray::TrayManager {
    icon: context.tray_icon,
    icons: Default::default(),

Nothing at the call site signals otherwise — the method name, the receiver type, and the adjacent correctly-scoped vector all point the wrong way.

```rust

        .setup(|app| {

### How this presented in a real app

It was invisible for a release, because the verbs that doubled were idempotent — window-opening actions that focus-or-create a fixed label, so a doubled dispatch appeared to produce one window. The codebase had reasoned about duplicate delivery, concluded it was harmless, and was correct for every case that existed at the time.

Two things were then found:

1. The first **non-idempotent** verb to route through it drew **two stacked native dialogs**, one behind the other. The user dismissed one and another appeared — which is how it was finally noticed.
2. The "idempotent" verbs were **not** idempotent either. Measured on a debug build: **2 duplicate windows in 7 single clicks**. That is a bug in the consuming app, not in Tauri — but the duplicate dispatch is what made it reachable, and the doubling is what turned a latent race into an observed one.

1. **Scope it.** Make `TrayIconBuilder::on_menu_event` deliver only events originating from that tray's menu. This matches what the name and receiver imply. ### Describe the bug

On Android, an `emit` that runs on the tao event-loop thread (for example from `AppHandle::run_on_main_thread`) can deadlock the Android UI thread and cause an ANR. `tauri-runtime-wry` keeps two mutexes locked across a call that blocks on wry's bounded `MainPipe` channel, and only the UI thread drains that channel.

We hit this in production through `tauri-plugin-powersync`, which forwards database table updates with `run_on_main_thread(|| app.emit(..))` (plugin-side issue: powersync-ja/powersync-js#1131). A burst of emits during an initial sync reliably fills the pipe.

Three threads, all from the same ANR dump (stacks trimmed, outermost first):

| Thread | Stack | Holds | Blocked on |
|---|---|---|---|
| tao event loop (`Thread-N`) | `EventLoop::run` → `handle_user_message` (the `run_on_main_thread` closure) → `AppHandle::emit` → `AppManager::emit` → `Listeners::emit_js_filter` → `Webview::emit_js` → `WryWebviewDispatcher::eval_script` → `send_user_message` → `handle_user_message` (inline, `current_thread() == main_thread_id`) → `wry::android::InnerWebView::eval` → `MainPipe::send` → `crossbeam_channel` array `send` → `park` | `webviews_lock()` and the `window_id` guard | a free slot in `MainPipe`'s `bounded(8)` channel |
| Android UI (`main`) | `Looper.loop` → `PluginManager.runCommand` → `Invoke.resolve` → `PluginManager.handlePluginResponse` (JNI) → `tauri::plugin::mobile::handle_android_plugin_response` → `InvokeResolver::return_result` → `handle_ipc_message::responder_eval` → `WryWebviewDispatcher::eval_script` → `Mutex::lock_contended` | — | `window_id` |
| `JavaBridge` | `Ipc.postMessage` → `wry::android::binding::ipc` → `tauri::ipc::protocol::message_handler` → `AppManager::get_webview` → `Mutex::lock_contended` | — | `webviews_lock` |

Where the locks are held (same code in 2.11.x and 2.12.0):

1. `tauri-runtime-wry` `WryWebviewDispatcher::eval_script` (non-`tracing` variant):
   ```rust
   self.context.send_user_message(Message::Webview(
     *self.window_id.lock().unwrap(),   // guard is a temporary: lives until send_user_message returns
     self.webview_id,
     WebviewMessage::EvaluateScript(script.into()),
   ))
   ```
   On the event-loop thread `send_user_message` runs `handle_user_message` inline, which ends up in `wry::android::InnerWebView::eval` → `MainPipe::send` → `CHANNEL.0.send(..)` on a `bounded(8)` channel. That send blocks while the `window_id` guard is still alive.
2. `tauri` `AppManager::emit`: `listeners.emit_js(self.webview.webviews_lock().values(), &emit_args)` keeps `webviews_lock` held for the whole `emit_js` → `eval_script` call. `emit_js_filter` also holds `js_event_listeners`.

The UI thread is the only consumer of `MainPipe`, but resolving any Kotlin plugin response goes through `eval_script`, which takes `window_id` first. That is a circular wait.

Emitting from a background (tokio) thread avoids it: there `send_user_message` takes the `proxy.send_event` → `try_send` path on tao's unbounded queue, every lock is released immediately, and the event-loop thread later blocks on the pipe without holding anything the UI thread needs. That is what we ship as a workaround, gated to Android.

### Reproduction

No minimal repro yet: it is timing-dependent and we only observe it on devices. The ingredients:

1. On Android, from the event-loop thread (`app.run_on_main_thread(..)`), call `app.emit(..)` in a burst (well over 8 events) while a webview has a JS listener for the event.
2. At the same time, trigger Kotlin plugin commands from JS (for example `addPluginListener` → `registerListener`), so the UI thread resolves invokes through `responder_eval` → `eval_script`.

The UI thread then parks in `eval_script` on `window_id` and Android reports an ANR after about 5 s.

### Expected behavior

`emit` / `eval_script` on the event-loop thread should never block on the UI thread while holding a lock that the UI thread's IPC path needs.

Possible fixes, any one of which breaks the cycle:
- Bind `let window_id = *self.window_id.lock().unwrap();` before calling `send_user_message` in `eval_script` (and in the sibling methods that use the same pattern).
- In `AppManager::emit`, collect the webviews (clone) before calling `emit_js` instead of holding `webviews_lock()` across it.
- On Android, never run `handle_user_message` inline for messages that end in `MainPipe::send` (always enqueue), or make `MainPipe::send` non-blocking from the event-loop thread.

### Full `tauri info` output

```text
[✔] Environment
    - OS: Mac OS 27.0.1 arm64 (X64)
    ✔ Xcode Command Line Tools: installed
    ✔ Xcode: 27.0
    ✔ rustc: 1.98.1 (48a229cea 2026-09-01)
    ✔ cargo: 1.98.1 (797e8a9bc 2026-08-05)
    ✔ rustup: 1.29.0 (28d1352db 2026-03-05)
    ✔ Rust toolchain: stable-aarch64-apple-darwin (default)
    - node: 26.3.1
    - bun: 1.3.14

[-] Packages
    - tauri 🦀: 2.11.5, (outdated, latest: 2.12.0)
    - tauri-build 🦀: 2.6.3, (outdated, latest: 2.7.0)
    - wry 🦀: 0.55.1, (outdated, latest: 0.57.0)
    - tao 🦀: 0.35.3, (outdated, latest: 0.37.1)
    - @tauri-apps/api  ⱼₛ: 2.11.1 (outdated, latest: 2.12.0)
    - @tauri-apps/cli  ⱼₛ: 2.11.4 (outdated, latest: 2.12.0)
```

`tauri-runtime-wry` is 2.11.4. I checked the 2.12.0 / 0.57.0 sources and the code paths above are unchanged. Target devices run Android 14 and 16 (arm64).

### Stack trace

See the table above. Main-thread frames reported by Sentry, innermost last:

```text
app.tauri.plugin.PluginManager.runCommand
app.tauri.plugin.Plugin.registerListener
app.tauri.plugin.Invoke.c
app.tauri.plugin.PluginManager.handlePluginResponse
Java_app_tauri_plugin_PluginManager_handlePluginResponse
tauri::plugin::mobile::handle_android_plugin_response
tauri::webview::Webview::on_message::{closure#2}
tauri::ipc::InvokeResolver::resolve
tauri::ipc::InvokeResolver::return_result
tauri::ipc::protocol::handle_ipc_message::{closure#1}::responder_eval
tauri_runtime_wry::WryWebviewDispatcher::eval_script
std::sys::sync::mutex::futex::Mutex::lock_contended
syscall
```

### Additional context

Related but distinct: #14694 (Android freeze with `AppManager::plugins` held across a main-thread round trip) and #15891 (AB-BA between a worker-held lock and a main-thread handler). The same class of bug, "lock held across a blocking hop to the UI thread", seems to appear in several places on Android because the event loop and the UI thread are different threads there.

### Describe the problem

On iOS, the Tauri CLI merges `src-tauri/Info.ios.plist` into the generated `Info.plist`. Custom keys thus stay when `tauri ios init` makes the project again.

Android has no equivalent. Custom entries must go directly into `src-tauri/gen/android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml`. When `tauri android init` makes the project again, these entries are lost. You must then add them again manually.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Merge `src-tauri/AndroidManifest.xml` into the generated manifest, as the CLI does for `Info.ios.plist`. Use the Gradle manifest merger, so that `tools:node` and `tools:replace` operate as usual. Do the merge before the Gradle build starts.

```xml
<manifest xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android">
    <application>
        <activity android:name=".MainActivity">
            <intent-filter>
                <action android:name="android.intent.action.SEND" />
                <category android:name="android.intent.category.DEFAULT" />
                <data android:mimeType="text/plain" />
            </intent-filter>
        </activity>
    </application>
</manifest>
```

### Alternatives considered

- **Restore the entries from Git after each `tauri android init`.** This is manual, and it is easy to make an error.
- **Call `update_android_manifest` from the build script.** This helper only adds text between marker comments, and it runs inside the Gradle build.

### Additional context

### Describe the bug

I updated from `2.11.6` to `2.12.1` and now images won't load in my app in dev mode. The console shows an error like:

```
Unsafe attempt to load URL asset://localhost/<yada yada yada> from origin http://localhost:1420/. Domains, protocols and ports must match.
```

Fetching the same asset url with `fetch('asset://localhost/<yada yada yada>').then(r => console.log(r.status, [...r.headers]))` on the console works fine. But loading a plain image in the console with:

```
const i = new Image()
i.onload = () => console.log('ok')
i.onerror = e => console.log('err', e)
i.src = 'asset://localhost/<yada yada yada>'
```

fails with the same "unsafe" error. The production build works fine.
