Protobuf schemas containing `google.protobuf.Struct` fields can't be queried through the Kafka connector. The schema parser rejects them with the error:

```
Protobuf schema containing fields with self-reference are not supported because they cannot be mapped to a Trino type
```

`google.protobuf.Struct`, `google.protobuf.Value`, and `google.protobuf.ListValue` are [well-known protobuf types][1] with a [defined JSON mapping][2] in the protobuf specification. They form a closed type family representing arbitrary JSON-like data:

- [`Struct`](https://protobuf.dev/reference/protobuf/google.protobuf/#struct) - JSON object (e.g., `map<string, Value>`)
- [`Value`](https://protobuf.dev/reference/protobuf/google.protobuf/#value) - any JSON value (`oneof` of `null`, `number`, `string`, `bool`, `Struct`,
  `ListValue`)
- [`ListValue`](https://protobuf.dev/reference/protobuf/google.protobuf/#list-value) - JSON array (`repeated Value`)

These types contain self references (`Struct` -> `Value` -> `Struct`), which triggers the [recursive type detection in `ProtobufSchemaParser`](https://github.com/trinodb/trino/blob/b8997c21a05bcc06d1f0dfd12e3fd528a925907e/plugin/trino-kafka/src/main/java/io/trino/plugin/kafka/encoder/protobuf/ProtobufSchemaParser.java#L154-L163). However, unlike arbitrary user-defined recursive messages (which may require an infinitely nested Trino row type), `Struct`, `Value`, and `ListValue` have a canonical JSON representation defined by the [protobuf JSON mapping specification][2] outlined above. They map naturally to Trino's JSON type, with serialization handled entirely by protobuf's `JsonFormat.printer()`, similar to the [existing treatment of the `Any` type](https://github.com/trinodb/trino/blob/b8997c21a05bcc06d1f0dfd12e3fd528a925907e/plugin/trino-kafka/src/main/java/io/trino/plugin/kafka/encoder/protobuf/ProtobufSchemaParser.java#L150-L152).

## Expected behavior

Fields of type `google.protobuf.Struct`, `Value`, or `ListValue` should be mapped to Trino's `JSON` type, following the same pattern used for `google.protobuf.Any` (mapped to JSON).

## Example schema that fails

```proto
syntax = "proto3";
import "google/protobuf/struct.proto";

message Event {
    string id = 1;
    google.protobuf.Struct metadata = 2;
}
```

Querying a Kafka topic using this schema produces the recursive type error instead of returning the `metadata` field as JSON.

[1]: https://protobuf.dev/reference/protobuf/google.protobuf/
[2]: https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/json/

body_text:
The [current docs on secure internal communication (479)](https://trino.io/docs/479/security/internal-communication.html) only mention the shared secret model for securing internal communication, where a shared secret is used to generate a TLS certificate on all nodes, rather than relying on a more traditional PKI setup where trust is established through a CA hierarchy. This shared secret model isn't compatible with the model of trust and identity my company is trying to enforce across its infrastructure.

Trino actually has options to use traditional PKI, with the (now undocumented) config options, `internal-communication.https.keystore.path`, and `internal-communication.https.truststore.path`. However, I hesitant to start using these options, as it's unclear how long they will continue to be supported for. It seems that the shared secret model is intended as a replacement for these options. Previous versions of the docs even mention removing these options as an "upgrade", see [412](https://trino.io/docs/412/security/internal-communication.html#).

I don't intend to start a debate over the security value of PKI vs. shared secrets here. I also understand that shared secrets are significantly easier for a large number of users to configure. However, I suspect my company isn't alone in strongly preferring PKI, in already having the ability to issue certificates to all nodes, and in being subject to compliance requirements that are more easily satisfied by the PKI model.

Would it be possible to bring these options back into the docs, and to continue to support them as a first-class method of securing internal communication?

body_text:
With connector guaranteeing limit/topN pushdown (like Postgres), queries involving order-by offset limit do not always output ordered results.

The issue seems to be that when the TopN is pushed though the connector, there is TopN in plan as expected.
StreamPropertyDerivations.visitRowNumber today is just a passthrough - but now the input is a gatherer not reporting orderered=true (LocalExchange[SINGLE]) - and ultimately those AddLocalExchanges to add this ROUND_ROBIN repartition which breaks the effective ordering.


AI generated reproducer/fix at https://github.com/freakyzoidberg/trino/commit/8c666da62712f61a7198ac3e5f46b82f8d0478dd

Thanks

body_text:
Compliant writers of Delta tables may optionally write "checksum" files alongside each commit. These checksum files contain a variety of (optional) useful information, including the Delta table metadata and protocol information. See https://github.com/delta-io/delta/blob/488c916931ca9d210f4cadd2d5520e0274d26b04/PROTOCOL.md#version-checksum-file for the full checksum file spec.

This information can be use to accelerate reading Delta Lake metadata information

Any comments will be welcome.

Applications/services can retrieve an access token from Microsoft Entra ID and use that to connect to Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed Instance, and Azure Synapse Analytics, Dataverse TDS endpoint etc..
The "accessToken" can only be set using the Properties parameter of the getConnection() method in the DriverManager class. It can't be used in the connection string.

The following query:

```sql
SELECT TYPE_NAME, DATA_TYPE from system.jdbc.types where type_name = 'char';
```
returns
 > char	2000

It should return 
>  char    1

The same issue applies to other types, like varchar. 

That causes JDBC method `DatabaseMetaData.getTypeInfo()` to return wrong values for `DATA_TYPE` and causes for instance the SQL `CHAR` type to be mapped to `JDBC_OBJECT` instead of `CHAR`.

body_text:
We are developing a high-throughput data connector using the Trino JDBC driver and benchmarked two write strategies:

1. Standard JDBC batching (`PreparedStatement.addBatch()` / `executeBatch()`)
2. JSON-based insert pattern (`json_parse(...)` + `UNNEST`)

### Performance findings

- **JDBC batching** is significantly slower and becomes a bottleneck for high-volume pipelines.
- **JSON + UNNEST** is approximately **3-4x faster**, reaching about **10k rows/sec** in our workload.

### Problem

The JSON approach provides better throughput but requires complex, brittle manual type handling for dynamic schemas (temporal precision, decimal precision/scale, varbinary/base64, identifier escaping, etc.).

For connector reliability and maintainability, we want competitive performance via standard JDBC APIs, without maintaining custom mapping utilities per source system.

### Upstream context

We also discussed this with jOOQ maintainers (jOOQ issue #19685). Their feedback was that jOOQ batch behavior is constrained by how Trino JDBC implements `executeBatch()`.

### Request

Please consider optimizing Trino JDBC batch processing to reduce the performance gap versus JSON-based ingestion.

We are specifically looking for guidance or improvements that allow efficient bulk transfers through standard JDBC usage, without application-level JSON serialization/deserialization workarounds.

**Related tickets:** https://github.com/trinodb/trino/issues/5913

body_text:
I am trying to run very simple query:

```
CREATE TABLE iceberg_catalog.my_schema.my_dest_table
  WITH (
         format = 'PARQUET',
         format_version = 2,
         location = 's3://my_bucket/my_schema/my_dest_table'
)
AS
SELECT * from iceberg_catalog.my_schema.my_source_table;
```

There can be variations: more complex query, partitions in tables but the problem appeared anyway.

Expected behaviour: 

1. Trino estimate input data
2. pick up a piece of data
3. process data
4. write a piece of process data
5. repeat 2 - 4 until all data processed

Expected behaviour: 

1. Trino reads all data in memory
2. Trino write all data to s3
3. If memory on a worker is not enough - it fails with `Encountered too many errors talking to a worker node`

Note about partitions

When destionation table has partitions writers are scalled much better. But anyway when a lot of data I have to add additional partition filed. For example if table partitioned by day and fails - I have to add bucketing for email `bucket(email, 10)` - so less data goes to worker and writing completed.

I have tried [writer properties](https://trino.io/docs/current/admin/properties-writer-scaling.html) but have no effect. Also there it is not mentioned that these setting have no effect when table have partitions.

**What is the problem in total**

There is no way to "say" to Trino: "slice data into N size butches" or "use this function to scale writes".

**Problem Statement:**
SHOW CREATE TABLE cmd for hive connector is returning managed table path as external_location causing confusion that the table is managed or external and violates the Principle of Least Surprise.

 **Steps to reproduce:**
1. Create a schema: 
`CREATE SCHEMA hive.some_hive`

2. Create a managed table: ""
`CREATE TABLE hive.some_hive.new_table(id int, name varchar);`

3. show create table  hive.some_hive.new_table;

**Current Output:**
`trino> show create table  hive.some_hive.new_table;`
`                                      Create Table                                `
`--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------`
`CREATE TABLE hive.some_hive.new_table (       `                                             
  `  id integer,             `                                                                
`    name varchar                     `                                                       
` )                  `                                                                        
` WITH (     `                                                                                
    `external_location = 'hdfs://localhost:9000/user/hive/warehouse/some_hive.db/new_table', `
    `format = 'ORC'                `                                                          
 `)         `                                                                                 
`(1 row)`

`Splits: 1 total, 1 done (100.00%)`
`0.37 [0 rows, 0B] [0 rows/s, 0B/s]`

`trino> `

**Expected output:**
The "external_location" keyword should be either "location" or it should not be present for managed table at all.

body_text:
After updating from Trino v444 to v479 we found that `MERGE INTO` queries that do a lot of updates in the target table create thousands of position delete files.

To reproduce,

1. Create an Iceberg table with more than one data file:

  ```sql
  create table faker.default.source
  (
      uid      uuid    not null,
      age      integer not null,
      name     VARCHAR NOT NULL WITH (generator = '#{Name.first_name} #{Name.last_name}'),
      address1 VARCHAR NOT NULL WITH (generator = '#{Address.fullAddress}'),
      address2 VARCHAR NOT NULL WITH (generator = '#{Address.fullAddress}'),
      address3 VARCHAR NOT NULL WITH (generator = '#{Address.fullAddress}'),
      enrolled BOOLEAN not null
  )
      with (default_limit = 10000000)
  ;
  
  create table iceberg.default.merge_target
  as
  select *
  from faker.default.source
  ;
  ```
  I was testing on a local `DevServer` with just two nodes (one coordinator with `node-scheduler.include-coordinator=true` and one worker) and in my case I got 14 data files:

  ```sql
  select content, count() as count
  from iceberg.default."merge_target$files"
  group by 1
  ```
  
  | content | count |
  | :--- | :--- |
  | 0 | 14 |

2. Create a delta table with ~1/10-th of the original UUIDs + a few new ones:

  ```sql
  create table iceberg.default.merge_delta
  as
  select *
  from iceberg.default.merge_target
  order by rand()
  limit 1000000
  ;
  
  insert into iceberg.default.merge_delta
  select *
  from faker.default.source
  limit 100000
  ;
  ```

3. Now, executing the following `MERGE INTO`:
  ```sql
  merge into iceberg.default.merge_target target
  using iceberg.default.merge_delta delta
    on target.uid = delta.uid
  when matched then update
      set uid = delta.uid,
          age = delta.age,
          name = delta.name,
          address1 = delta.address1,
          address2 = delta.address2,
          address3 = delta.address3,
          enrolled = delta.enrolled
  when not matched then insert
      (uid,
       age,
       name,
       address1,
       address2,
       address3,
       enrolled)
      values (delta.uid,
              delta.age,
              delta.name,
              delta.address1,
              delta.address2,
              delta.address3,
              delta.enrolled)
  ;
  ```
  
  ends up writing 2 new data files and 28 position delete files:
  
  ```sql
  select content, count() as count
  from iceberg.default."merge_target$files"
  group by 1
  ```
  
  | content | count |
  | :--- | :--- |
  | 0 | 16 |
  | 1 | 28 |

The `min(number of workers, 100) × number of data files` upper limit seems to apply to our production cluster as well — for example, today a `MERGE INTO` query updating a table with ~540M rows across 1367 data files, running on 160 workers, added
* 3.39M rows in 100 data files, and
* 3.36M position delete rows in **115923 delete files** — fairly close to 100×1367

---

I was able to bisect the git history and find the culprit commit: [3359c28](https://github.com/trinodb/trino/commit/3359c280ebf610b3fde8dd30958120158a8b951a) from https://github.com/trinodb/trino/pull/23432, released with Trino v468. The same test query running on [its parent](https://github.com/trinodb/trino/commit/52d5f78e3541d06ad637b77ccff54ebec3008dac) creates 4 data and, as expected, 14 delete files.

The difference, as far as I can tell, is that the output from `MergeProcessor` in stage 2 was being partitioned by the operation code and location of the row in the original data files (`field`) before:

```
...

Fragment 2 [HASH]
    Output layout: [..., operation, case_number_26, field, insert_from_update]
    Output partitioning: MERGE [update = iceberg:INSTANCE] [operation, field]
    MergeProcessor[]
    ...
```

and after it became round robin with 100 partitions:

```
...
Fragment 2 [HASH]
    Output layout: [..., operation, case_number_26, field, insert_from_update]
    Output partitioning: ROUND_ROBIN []
    Output partition count: 100
    MergeProcessor[]
    ...
```

After Trino v468, at some point the `MergeProcessor` started being merged with `MergeWriter` via `LocalExchange` in the same stage, so the relevant part of the plan looks like this on v479:

```
...
Fragment 1 [HASH]
    Output layout: [partialrows, fragment]
    Output partitioning: SINGLE []
    MergeWriter[table = iceberg:default.merge_target$data@2949827968648840322]
    │   Layout: [partialrows:bigint, fragment:varbinary]
    └─ LocalExchange[partitioning = SINGLE]
       │   Layout: [..., operation:tinyint, case_number_27:integer, field:row(_file varchar, _pos bigint, partition_spec_id integer, partition_data varchar), insert_from_update:tinyint]
       │   Estimates: {rows: ? (?), cpu: 0, memory: 0B, network: 0B}
       └─ MergeProcessor[]
          │   Layout: [..., operation:tinyint, case_number_27:integer, field:row(_file varchar, _pos bigint, partition_spec_id integer, partition_data varchar), insert_from_update:tinyint]
          │   target: iceberg:default.merge_target$data@2949827968648840322
          │   merge row column: merge_row
          │   row id column: field
          │   redistribution columns: []
...
```

Disabling the feature introduced in #23432 by setting `iceberg.bucket_execution_enabled` to `false` doesn’t help, which, I think, is expected.

Of course, delete vectors cannot come soon enough, but is there anything that can be done to help in this case with v2?

body_text:
### Problem

Until Trino version 431, we were able to restrict access to UDFs located in the plugins folder. However, in the newer versions, these UDFs appear under system.builtin functions, making them accessible to all users by default.

Is there a way to enforce access control rules on these UDFs similar to how it worked in earlier versions? If this capability is not currently available, can access rules enforcement be added for these functions as well?

### Proposed Solution

Adding the UDFs present in plugin directory to **_system.<plugin-name>_** schema. And add these **_system.<plugin-name>_** to the sqlPaths so that these functions will be resolved without specifying the whole catalog schema function name.

### Impact 
Will be able to restrict the UDFs from plugins using access control properties

When using the Cassandra connector with partition keys that are INT or BIGINT, specifying multiple consecutive values using the IN clause or OR operator causes them to be expanded into BETWEEN clauses.

However, Cassandra cannot perform partition key filtering on queries using BETWEEN with INT keys.

Consequently, when attempting to retrieve multiple partitions from an INT partition key, the connector retrieves all partitions even in cases where filtering should be possible.

For example, suppose the partition_key column contains values 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.

Queries like `WHERE partition_column = 1` or `WHERE partition_column IN (1, 3, 5)` work fine.
However, queries like `WHERE partition_column IN (1,2,3,4)` are converted to `BETWEEN 1 AND 4`, resulting in a full scan.

## Description
### Problem
Currently, the file-based system access control requires catalog-level ALL access mode to execute SHOW CREATE TABLE, even though this is a read-only metadata operation. This prevents organizations from allowing users to view table DDL without also granting them permissions to create, drop, or modify tables.

### Current Behavior
In FileBasedSystemAccessControl.java, the checkCanShowCreateTable method requires the OWNERSHIP table privilege:

```
@Override
public void checkCanShowCreateTable(SystemSecurityContext context, CatalogSchemaTableName table)
{
    if (!checkTablePermission(context, table, OWNERSHIP)) {
        denyShowCreateTable(table.toString());
    }
}
```

However, checkTablePermission enforces catalog-level ALL access for any privilege other than SELECT or GRANT_SELECT:

```
private boolean checkTablePermission(SystemSecurityContext context, CatalogSchemaTableName table, TableAccessControlRule.TablePrivilege requiredPrivilege)
{
    AccessMode requiredCatalogAccess = requiredPrivilege == SELECT || requiredPrivilege == GRANT_SELECT ? READ_ONLY : ALL;
    return checkTablePermission(context, table, requiredCatalogAccess, privileges -> privileges.contains(requiredPrivilege));
}
```

This means users with catalog-level READ_ONLY access cannot execute SHOW CREATE TABLE, even if they have table-level OWNERSHIP privileges.

### Expected Behavior
SHOW CREATE TABLE should be allowed with catalog-level READ_ONLY access, as it's a read-only metadata operation that doesn't modify any data or schema objects.

### Use Case
Organizations want to allow data analysts and developers to:

- ✅ View table schemas and DDL (SHOW CREATE TABLE)
- ✅ Query data (SELECT)
- ❌ Create new tables (CREATE TABLE)
- ❌ Drop or modify tables (DROP TABLE, ALTER TABLE)

This is a common security pattern where users need to understand table structure for querying purposes without having write permissions.

### Proposed Solution
Introduce a new table privilege (e.g., SHOW_CREATE or VIEW_METADATA) that:

1. Allows SHOW CREATE TABLE operations
2. Only requires catalog-level READ_ONLY access
3. Does not grant any write or modification permissions

Alternatively, treat SHOW CREATE TABLE as a read-only operation that only requires SELECT privilege, similar to how SHOW COLUMNS works.

### Workarounds
Currently, the only workarounds are:

1. Grant catalog-level ALL access (security risk - allows table creation/deletion)
2. Use a different access control system like Apache Ranger or OPA
3. Deny users the ability to view table DDL

### Environment
Trino version: 479 (tested on latest master)

Access control: file-based system access control

Configuration: rules.json with catalog and table rules

### Additional Context
This limitation affects the usability of file-based access control for organizations that want fine-grained read permissions without granting write access. The current coupling of metadata viewing with write permissions is overly restrictive for read-only use cases.

### Trino version

>478

### Please describe the bug

After upgrading to Trino 478, the Oracle connector is no longer able to execute queries successfully.
Any query sent to Oracle through Trino fails with the following error:

```
SQL Error [67108864]: Query failed (#20260315_XXXXX): ORA-00933: SQL command not properly ended
Oracle error reference: https://docs.oracle.com/error-help/db/ora-00933/
```
The same queries execute successfully when run directly against the Oracle database using native Oracle tools.

Steps to reproduce

Configure Trino with the Oracle connector.

Connect to an Oracle schema.

Execute a simple query, for example:

`SELECT * FROM schema.table_name;
`
Expected behavior

The query should execute normally and return results from Oracle.

Actual behavior

The query fails with:

`SQL Error [67108864]: Query failed (#20260315_XXXXX): ORA-00933: SQL command not properly ended
`

Additional context

The issue occurs with all queries, including simple SELECT statements.

Queries run successfully when executed directly in Oracle (SQL*Plus / SQL Developer).

This behavior started after using Trino version 478.
